In the Likeness of a Dream
A modern-English rendering of John Bunyan's 1678 original. Character and place names are kept exactly as Bunyan wrote them. Bunyan's own Scripture references are kept in brackets.

As I walked through the wilderness of this world, I came to a certain place where there was a den, and I lay down there to sleep; and as I slept, I dreamed a dream. I dreamed, and look — I saw a man clothed in rags, standing in a certain place with his face turned away from his own house, a book in his hand, and a great burden on his back. [Isa. 64:6; Luke 14:33; Ps. 38:4; Hab. 2:2; Acts 16:30,31] I looked and saw him open the book and read in it; and as he read, he wept and trembled; and, no longer able to hold it in, he broke out with a sorrowful cry, saying, "What shall I do?" [Acts 2:37]

In this state, then, he went home and held himself in as long as he could, so that his wife and children would not notice his distress; but he could not stay silent for long, because his trouble kept growing. So at last he opened his mind to his wife and children, and began to talk to them like this: "O my dear wife," he said, "and you, the children I love, I, your dear friend, am ruined within myself because of a burden that lies heavy on me. What's more, I have been told for certain that this city of ours will be burned with fire from heaven, and in that dreadful destruction both I and you, my wife, and you, my sweet children, will all be miserably ruined — unless (and I do not yet see how) some way of escape can be found by which we may be delivered." At this his family was deeply alarmed — not because they believed what he told them was true, but because they thought some kind of madness had taken hold of his mind. So, since it was getting toward night and they hoped sleep might settle his brain, they hurried him off to bed. But the night was as troubled for him as the day had been; so instead of sleeping, he spent it in sighs and tears. When morning came, they wanted to know how he was. He told them, "Worse and worse." He also began to talk to them again, but they began to harden themselves. They tried to drive away his trouble by treating him harshly and rudely: sometimes they mocked him, sometimes they scolded him, and sometimes they simply ignored him. So he began to withdraw to his room — to pray for them and pity them, and also to grieve over his own misery. He would also walk alone in the fields, sometimes reading and sometimes praying; and so he spent his time for several days.

Now I saw that one day, while he was walking in the fields, he was reading in his book as usual and was greatly distressed in his mind; and as he read, he burst out as he had before, crying, "What shall I do to be saved?"

I saw also that he looked this way and that, as if he wanted to run, and yet he stood still, because (as I could see) he could not tell which way to go. Then I looked and saw a man named Evangelist coming toward him, and he asked, "Why are you crying out?" [Job 33:23]

He answered, "Sir, I can see from the book in my hand that I am condemned to die, and after that to face judgment [Heb. 9:27]; and I find that I am not willing to do the first [Job 16:21], nor able to do the second." [Ezek. 22:14]
Christian no sooner leaves the World but meets
Evangelist, who lovingly him greets
With tidings of another; and does show
Him how to climb to that from this below.

Then Evangelist said, "Why are you unwilling to die, since this life is full of so many troubles?" The man answered, "Because I am afraid that this burden on my back will sink me lower than the grave, and I shall fall into Tophet. [Isa. 30:33] And, sir, if I am not fit to go to prison, then I am surely not fit to go to judgment, and from there to execution; and the thought of these things makes me cry out."

Then Evangelist said, "If this is your condition, why are you standing still?" He answered, "Because I don't know where to go." Then Evangelist gave him a parchment scroll, and written on it were the words: Flee from the wrath to come. [Matt. 3:7]

So the man read it, and looking very carefully at Evangelist, said, "Where must I flee?" Then Evangelist, pointing with his finger across a very wide field, said, "Do you see that wicket-gate over there?" [Matt. 7:13,14] The man said, "No." Then Evangelist said, "Do you see that shining light over there?" [Ps. 119:105; 2 Pet. 1:19] He said, "I think I do." Then Evangelist said, "Keep that light in your eye, and go straight up toward it; then you will see the gate. When you knock there, you will be told what you must do."
So in my dream I saw the man begin to run.

Now he had not run far from his own door when his wife and children, seeing him go, began to cry out after him to come back. But the man put his fingers in his ears and ran on, crying, "Life! Life! Eternal life!" [Luke 14:26] So he did not look behind him, but fled toward the middle of the plain. [Gen. 19:17]

The neighbors also came out to watch him run [Jer. 20:10], and as he ran, some mocked, others threatened, and some called after him to come back; and among those who did so were two who decided to bring him back by force. The name of the one was Obstinate, and the name of the other was Pliable. By this time the man had gotten a good distance from them, but they were determined to chase after him, which they did, and in a little while they caught up with him. Then the man said, "Neighbors, why have you come?" They said, "To persuade you to go back with us." But he said, "That can never be. You live in the City of Destruction — the place where I too was born — and I can see that it is so; and dying there, sooner or later, you will sink lower than the grave, into a place that burns with fire and brimstone. Be reasonable, good neighbors, and come along with me."
Obstinate: "What!" said Obstinate. "And leave our friends and our comforts behind us?"

Christian: "Yes," said Christian (for that was his name), "because everything you would give up is not worth comparing to even a little of what I am seeking to enjoy. [2 Cor. 4:18] And if you come along with me and hold to it, you will fare as I do; for where I am going there is more than enough to spare. [Luke 15:17] Come along, and test my words for yourselves."
Obstinate: "What are these things you're looking for, that you would leave the whole world to find them?"

Christian: "I am looking for an inheritance that can never perish, spoil, or fade [1 Pet. 1:4]. It is kept safe in heaven [Heb. 11:16], to be given, at the appointed time, to those who diligently seek it. Read it for yourself, if you like, here in my book."
Obstinate: "Nonsense!" said Obstinate. "Away with your book. Will you go back with us or not?"
Christian: "No, not I," said the other, "because I have put my hand to the plough." [Luke 9:62]

Obstinate: "Come on then, neighbor Pliable, let's turn around and go home without him. There's a whole crowd of these crazy-headed fools who, once they get a notion into their heads, think themselves wiser than seven men who can give a sensible reason." [Prov. 26:16]
Pliable: Then Pliable said, "Don't be so harsh. If what the good Christian says is true, then the things he's after are better than ours. My heart is inclined to go with my neighbor."
Obstinate: "What, more fools still! Take my advice and go back. Who knows where such a brain-sick fellow will lead you? Go back, go back, and be wise."

Christian: "No — come along with your neighbor, Pliable. There really are such things to be had as I spoke of, and many more glorious besides. If you don't believe me, read here in this book; and as for the truth of what is written in it, look — it is all confirmed by the blood of the One who made it." [Heb. 9:17-22; 13:20]

Pliable: "Well, neighbor Obstinate," said Pliable, "I'm beginning to make up my mind. I intend to go along with this good man and throw in my lot with him. But, my good companion, do you know the way to this place you long for?"
Christian: "I have been directed by a man named Evangelist to hurry to a little gate up ahead of us, where we will be given instructions about the way."
Pliable: "Come on then, good neighbor, let's get going." So the two of them went on together.
Obstinate: "And I will go back to my place," said Obstinate. "I won't be the companion of such misled, fanciful fellows."
Now I saw in my dream that when Obstinate had gone back, Christian and Pliable went on talking across the plain; and this is how their conversation began.

Christian: "Come, neighbor Pliable, how are you? I'm glad you were persuaded to come along with me. If Obstinate himself had felt what I have felt of the power and terror of things still unseen, he would not have turned his back on us so lightly."
Pliable: "Come, neighbor Christian, since there's no one here but the two of us, tell me more about what these things are, and how they are to be enjoyed, where we are going."

Christian: "I can picture them in my mind better than I can speak of them with my tongue. They are things of God, beyond words. But still, since you want to know, I will read about them from my book."
Pliable: "And do you really think the words of your book are certainly true?"
Christian: "Yes, truly; for it was made by the One who cannot lie." [Titus 1:2]
Pliable: "Well said. What things are they?"
Christian: "There is an endless kingdom to live in, and everlasting life to be given to us, so that we may live in that kingdom forever." [Isa. 45:17; John 10:28,29]
Pliable: "Well said. And what else?"
Christian: "There are crowns of glory to be given to us, and clothing that will make us shine like the sun in the sky of heaven." [2 Tim. 4:8; Rev. 3:4; Matt. 13:43]
Pliable: "That sounds wonderful. And what else?"
Christian: "There will be no more crying or sorrow, for the One who owns the place will wipe every tear from our eyes." [Isa. 25:6-8; Rev. 7:17, 21:4]
Pliable: "And what kind of company will we have there?"

Christian: "There we will be with seraphim and cherubim — creatures so bright they will dazzle your eyes to look at them. [Isa. 6:2] There too you will meet thousands upon thousands who have gone ahead of us to that place; none of them are harmful, but loving and holy, every one walking in the sight of God and standing in his presence, accepted forever. [1 Thess. 4:16,17; Rev. 5:11] In a word, there we will see the elders with their golden crowns [Rev. 4:4]; there we will see the holy ones with their golden harps [Rev. 14:1-5]; there we will see people who were cut to pieces by the world, burned in flames, eaten by beasts, and drowned in the seas for the love they bore to the Lord of that place — all of them well, and clothed with immortality as with a garment." [John 12:25; 2 Cor. 5:4]
Pliable: "Just hearing this is enough to thrill the heart! But are these things really to be had? How do we get to share in them?"
Christian: "The Lord, the Governor of that country, has written it down in this book; and the gist of it is this: if we are truly willing to have it, he will give it to us freely."
Pliable: "Well, my good companion, I'm glad to hear of these things. Come on, let's pick up the pace."
Christian: "I can't go as fast as I'd like, because of this burden on my back."

Now I saw in my dream that, just as they finished this conversation, they came near a very muddy bog in the middle of the plain; and being careless, they both suddenly fell into it. The name of the bog was Despond. So there they wallowed for a time, badly smeared with the mud; and Christian, because of the burden on his back, began to sink into the mire.
Pliable: Then Pliable said, "Ah, neighbor Christian, where are you now?"
Christian: "Truly," said Christian, "I do not know."

Pliable: At this Pliable began to take offense, and said angrily to his companion, "Is this the happiness you've been telling me about all this while? If we have such bad luck at our very first setting out, what can we expect between here and the end of our journey? If I get out of here alive, you can have that fine country to yourself for all I care." And with that he gave a desperate struggle or two and climbed out of the mire on the side of the bog nearest his own house; and away he went, and Christian saw him no more.

So Christian was left to flounder in the Slough of Despond alone. Still, he kept trying to struggle toward the side of the bog that was farther from his own house and nearer the wicket-gate; and this he did, but he could not get out, because of the burden on his back. But I saw in my dream that a man came to him whose name was Help, and asked him what he was doing there.

Christian: "Sir," said Christian, "I was told to go this way by a man called Evangelist, who also directed me to that gate over there, so that I might escape the wrath to come; and as I was going there, I fell in here."
Help: "But why didn't you look for the steps?"
Christian: "Fear was chasing me so hard that I fled the nearest way, and fell in."
Help: Then he said, "Give me your hand." So Christian gave him his hand, and Help drew him out and set him on solid ground, and told him to go on his way. [Ps. 40:2]

Then I went over to the one who had pulled him out, and said, "Sir, since this place is on the way from the City of Destruction to that gate, why is this patch of ground not repaired, so that poor travelers might go there more safely?" And he said to me, "This muddy bog is a place that cannot be repaired. It is the low spot where the scum and filth that come with conviction of sin keep draining down, and that is why it is called the Slough of Despond. For as the sinner is awakened to his lost condition, many fears and doubts and discouraging worries rise up in his soul, and all of them gather and settle in this place. That is why the ground here is so bad.

"It is not the King's wish that this place should stay so bad. [Isa. 35:3,4] His workers, too, on instructions from His Majesty's surveyors, have been busy with this patch of ground for more than sixteen hundred years, to see whether it might be repaired. In fact, to my own knowledge, at least twenty thousand cartloads — yes, millions — of wholesome instructions have been swallowed up here, brought in every season from all over the King's dominions; and those who know say these are the best materials for making the ground good, if it could be repaired. But it is the Slough of Despond still, and it will remain so when they have done all they can.

"It's true that, by the Lawgiver's direction, there are certain good and solid steps placed right through the middle of this bog. But at times when the place spews out its filth, as it does when the weather changes, those steps can hardly be seen; or, if they can, people get so dizzy-headed that they step off to the side, and then they get thoroughly bogged down, even though the steps are there. But the ground is good once they have made it in through the gate." [1 Sam. 12:23]

Now I saw in my dream that by this time Pliable had gotten home to his house again, so his neighbors came to visit him. Some of them called him a wise man for coming back, and some called him a fool for risking himself with Christian; and others mocked his cowardice, saying, "Surely, once you'd started out to venture, I wouldn't have been so spineless as to give up over a few difficulties." So Pliable sat there sheepish among them. But at last he got more confidence, and then they all changed their tune and began to mock poor Christian behind his back. And that's enough about Pliable.

Now, as Christian was walking by himself, he noticed someone far off, crossing the field to meet him; and it so happened that they met just as their paths crossed. The gentleman's name who met him was Mr. Worldly Wiseman, and he lived in the town of Carnal Policy, a very large town, and also quite near the place Christian had come from. This man, meeting Christian and having some idea of who he was — for Christian's setting out from the City of Destruction had been much talked about, not only in the town where he lived but in other places too — Mr. Worldly Wiseman, having some guess about him from watching his laborious walk and noticing his sighs and groans and the like, began to talk with Christian like this.
Worldly Wiseman: "How now, good fellow! Where are you off to, in this burdened state?"

Christian: "A burdened state indeed, as great, I think, as ever a poor creature had! And since you ask me where I'm off to, I'll tell you, sir: I am going to that wicket-gate up ahead of me; for there, as I have been told, I will be put on a path to be rid of my heavy burden."
Worldly Wiseman: "Do you have a wife and children?"
Christian: "Yes; but I am so weighed down with this burden that I can't take the pleasure in them that I used to. It feels as if I had none at all." [1 Cor. 7:29]
Worldly Wiseman: "Will you listen to me if I give you some advice?"
Christian: "If it's good advice, I will; for I am in need of good advice."

Worldly Wiseman: "Then I would advise you to get yourself rid of that burden as fast as you can; for you'll never be settled in your mind until you do, nor can you enjoy the blessings God has given you until then."

Christian: "That's exactly what I'm looking for — to be rid of this heavy burden. But I can't get it off myself, and there's no man in our country who can take it off my shoulders; and that is why I'm going this way, as I told you, so that I may be rid of my burden."
Worldly Wiseman: "Who told you to go this way to be rid of your burden?"
Christian: "A man who seemed to me to be a great and honorable person. His name, as I recall, is Evangelist."

Worldly Wiseman: "A curse on him for that advice! There is no more dangerous and troublesome road in the world than the one he has pointed you to, as you'll find out if you let his advice rule you. I see you've already met with something, for I can see the dirt of the Slough of Despond on you — and that bog is only the beginning of the sorrows that wait for those who go on that way. Listen to me, I'm older than you: on the road you're taking, you're likely to meet with weariness, pain, hunger, dangers, nakedness, sword, lions, dragons, darkness — and, in a word, death, and who knows what else! These things are certainly true, confirmed by many witnesses. So why should a man so carelessly throw himself away by listening to a stranger?"

Christian: "Why, sir, this burden on my back is more terrible to me than all the things you've mentioned. In fact, I don't care what I meet on the way, if only I can also meet with deliverance from my burden."
Worldly Wiseman: "How did you come by this burden in the first place?"
Christian: "By reading this book in my hand."

Worldly Wiseman: "I thought so. The same thing has happened to you as to other weak men who, meddling with matters too high for them, suddenly fall into the kind of distress you're in — which not only unmans them, as I can see it has done to you, but also drives them into desperate ventures to gain they-know-not-what."
Christian: "I know what I want to gain: relief from my heavy burden."

Worldly Wiseman: "But why look for relief this way, when so many dangers come with it? Especially since — if you had the patience to hear me out — I could point you to a way of getting what you want without the dangers you'll run into on this road. In fact, the remedy is close at hand. And I'll add this: instead of those dangers, you'll meet with plenty of safety, friendship, and contentment."
Christian: "Please, sir, share this secret with me."

Worldly Wiseman: "Why, in that village over there — the village is called Morality — there lives a gentleman named Legality, a very sensible man with a very good reputation, who has the skill to help people off with burdens like yours. To my own knowledge, he has done a great deal of good this way; and besides, he has the skill to cure those who have gone a bit cracked in their wits under their burdens. You can go to him, as I said, and be helped right away. His house is less than a mile from here; and if he should not be at home himself, he has a fine young son named Civility who can do it just as well as the old gentleman himself. There, I tell you, you can be relieved of your burden; and if you don't care to go back to your old home — which, frankly, I wouldn't advise — you can send for your wife and children to join you in this village, where there are houses standing empty that you could have at a reasonable rate. Provisions there are cheap and good too; and what will make your life all the happier is that you'll be living among honest neighbors, in good standing and respectability."
Now Christian was somewhat at a loss; but presently he concluded, "If what this gentleman says is true, my wisest course is to take his advice." And with that he spoke again.
Christian: "Sir, which is the way to this honest man's house?"
Worldly Wiseman: "Do you see that hill over there?"
Christian: "Yes, very well."
Worldly Wiseman: "Go by that hill, and the first house you come to is his."

So Christian turned out of his way to go to Mr. Legality's house for help. But look — when he had gotten close to the hill, it seemed so high, and the side of it next to the road hung over so far, that Christian was afraid to go any further, in case the hill should fall on his head. So there he stood still, not knowing what to do. His burden, too, now seemed heavier to him than while he was on his proper way. There came flashes of fire out of the hill as well, that made Christian afraid he would be burned. [Ex. 19:16,18] So there he stood sweating and quaking with fear. [Heb. 12:21]
When Christians lend their ear to worldly men,
They leave their way, and pay for it again;
For Mr. Worldly Wiseman can but show
A saint the road to bondage and to woe.

And now he began to be sorry that he had taken Mr. Worldly Wiseman's advice. And just then he saw Evangelist coming to meet him, and at the sight of him he began to blush with shame. So Evangelist came nearer and nearer; and coming up to him, he looked at him with a stern and dreadful expression, and began to reason with Christian like this.

Evangelist: "What are you doing here, Christian?" he said. At these words Christian did not know what to answer, so for the moment he stood speechless before him. Then Evangelist went on, "Aren't you the man I found crying outside the walls of the City of Destruction?"
Christian: "Yes, dear sir, I am that man."
Evangelist: "Didn't I direct you to the way of the little wicket-gate?"
Christian: "Yes, dear sir," said Christian.
Evangelist: "How is it, then, that you have turned aside so quickly? For you are now off the way."
Christian: "As soon as I had gotten over the Slough of Despond, I met a gentleman who persuaded me that in the village ahead I might find a man who would take off my burden."
Evangelist: "What was he?"

Christian: "He looked like a gentleman, and talked with me a good deal, and finally got me to give in; so I came here. But when I saw this hill, and how it hangs over the way, I suddenly stopped, in case it should fall on my head."
Evangelist: "What did that gentleman say to you?"
Christian: "Why, he asked me where I was going, and I told him."
Evangelist: "And what did he say then?"
Christian: "He asked me if I had a family, and I told him. But I said I am so weighed down with the burden on my back that I can't take pleasure in them as I used to."
Evangelist: "And what did he say then?"

Christian: "He told me to get rid of my burden quickly. I told him that relief was what I was looking for, and that I was therefore going to that gate over there to get further direction on how to reach the place of deliverance. So he said he would show me a better and shorter way, one not so full of difficulties as the way you set me in, sir — a way, he said, that would lead me to a gentleman's house, where someone had the skill to take off these burdens. So I believed him and turned out of that way into this one, hoping I might soon be relieved of my burden. But when I came to this place and saw things as they are, I stopped for fear of danger, as I said; and now I don't know what to do."

Evangelist: Then Evangelist said, "Stand still a moment, so that I may show you the words of God." So he stood there trembling. Then Evangelist said, "See that you do not refuse him who speaks. For if those did not escape who refused him who warned them on earth, much less shall we escape if we turn away from him who warns us from heaven." [Heb. 12:25] He said further, "Now the just shall live by faith; but if any man draw back, my soul shall have no pleasure in him." [Heb. 10:38] And he applied the words like this: "You are the man who is running into this misery. You have begun to reject the counsel of the Most High and to draw your foot back from the way of peace — to the point of very nearly throwing away your soul."

Then Christian fell down at his feet as if dead, crying, "Woe is me, for I am ruined!" Seeing this, Evangelist caught him by the right hand, saying, "All kinds of sin and blasphemy will be forgiven to men. [Matt. 12:31; Mark 3:28] Do not be faithless, but believing." [John 20:27] Then Christian revived a little, and stood up trembling, as he had at first, before Evangelist.

Then Evangelist went on: "Pay closer attention to the things I am about to tell you. I will show you who it was that deceived you, and who it was he sent you to. The man you met is one Worldly Wiseman, and the name fits him: partly because he relishes only the teaching of this world [1 John 4:5] (which is why he always goes to the town of Morality to church), and partly because he loves that teaching best, since it saves him best from the cross. [Gal. 6:12] And because he is of this worldly temper, he tries to twist my ways, right though they are. Now there are three things in this man's advice that you must utterly detest: first, his turning you out of the way; second, his working to make the cross hateful to you; and third, his setting your feet on the path that leads to death.

"First, you must detest his turning you out of the way, and your own agreeing to it — because that means rejecting the counsel of God for the sake of the counsel of a Worldly Wiseman. The Lord says, 'Strive to enter in at the strait gate' [Luke 13:24] — the gate I sent you to — 'for narrow is the gate that leads to life, and few there are that find it.' [Matt. 7:14] This wicked man has turned you away from that little wicket-gate, and from the way to it, and brought you almost to ruin. So hate his turning you out of the way, and despise yourself for listening to him.

"Second, you must detest his working to make the cross hateful to you, for you are to value it 'above the treasures of Egypt.' [Heb. 11:25,26] Besides, the King of glory has told you that whoever 'will save his life shall lose it' [Mark 8:35; John 12:25; Matt. 10:39], and that 'whoever comes after me, and does not hate his father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, yes, and his own life also, cannot be my disciple.' [Luke 14:26] So when a man works to persuade you that the very thing without which (the Truth has said) you cannot have eternal life will be your death — that teaching you must detest.

"Third, you must hate his setting your feet on the path that leads to death. For this, consider who he sent you to, and how unable that person was to deliver you from your burden. The man you were sent to for relief, named Legality, is the son of the slave-woman who is in bondage with her children [Gal. 4:21-27]; and he is, in a mystery, this Mount Sinai, which you feared would fall on your head. Now if she and her children are in bondage, how can you expect to be set free by them? This Legality, then, cannot free you from your burden. No man was ever yet rid of his burden by him, and none ever will be. You cannot be justified by the works of the law, for by the deeds of the law no living person can be rid of his burden. So Mr. Worldly Wiseman is a stranger to the truth, and Mr. Legality is a cheat; and as for his son Civility, for all his pleasant looks, he is only a hypocrite and cannot help you. Believe me, there is nothing in all this talk you have heard from these foolish men but a scheme to rob you of your salvation by turning you from the way I set you in." And with that Evangelist called aloud to the heavens for confirmation of what he had said; and there came words and fire out of the mountain under which poor Christian stood, that made the hair on his body stand up. The words were these: "As many as are of the works of the law are under the curse; for it is written, Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all the things written in the book of the law, to do them." [Gal. 3:10]

Now Christian expected nothing but death, and began to cry out miserably, cursing the time he had met Mr. Worldly Wiseman and calling himself a thousand fools for listening to him. He was deeply ashamed to think that this gentleman's arguments, springing only from the flesh, had carried such weight with him as to make him abandon the right way. Then he turned again to Evangelist and spoke:

Christian: "Sir, what do you think? Is there hope? May I go back now and go up to the wicket-gate? Will I not be turned away for this, and sent back ashamed? I am sorry I listened to that man's advice. But can my sin be forgiven?"

Evangelist: Then Evangelist said to him, "Your sin is very great, for by it you have committed two evils: you forsook the good way to walk in forbidden paths. Yet the man at the gate will receive you, for he has goodwill toward all people. Only take care that you do not turn aside again, 'lest you perish from the way when his wrath is kindled but a little.'" [Ps. 2:12] Then Christian set himself to go back; and Evangelist, after he had kissed him, gave him one smile and wished him Godspeed. So Christian went on in haste, and would neither speak to anyone along the way nor, if anyone asked him a question, give them an answer. He walked like a man treading on forbidden ground, and could not think himself safe until he was back on the way he had left to follow Mr. Worldly Wiseman's advice. So in time Christian came up to the gate. Now over the gate was written, "Knock, and it shall be opened to you." [Matt. 7:8]
Whoever would go in must first, without,
Stand knocking at the gate, nor need he doubt
That is a knocker but to enter in;
For God can love him, and forgive his sin.
So he knocked, more than once or twice, saying:
May I now enter here? Will he within
Open to sorry me, though I have been
An undeserving rebel? Then shall I
Not fail to sing his lasting praise on high.
At last a solemn man came to the gate, named Good-will, who asked who was there, where he had come from, and what he wanted.

Christian: "Here is a poor burdened sinner. I come from the City of Destruction, but I am going to Mount Zion, so that I may be delivered from the wrath to come. And since I am told that the way there is through this gate, I would like to know, sir, whether you are willing to let me in."
Good-will: "I am willing with all my heart," he said; and with that he opened the gate.

So as Christian was stepping in, the other gave him a pull. "What does that mean?" said Christian. The other told him: "A little distance from this gate stands a strong castle, of which Beelzebub is the captain. From there, both he and those with him shoot arrows at people coming up to this gate, in the hope that they may die before they get in."
Then Christian said, "I rejoice and tremble." So when he had gotten in, the keeper of the gate asked him who had directed him there.
Christian: "Evangelist told me to come here and knock, which I did; and he said that you, sir, would tell me what I must do."
Good-will: "An open door is set before you, and no one can shut it."
Christian: "Now I begin to reap the benefit of the risks I took."
Good-will: "But how is it that you came alone?"
Christian: "Because none of my neighbors saw their danger as I saw mine."
Good-will: "Did any of them know you were coming?"

Christian: "Yes; my wife and children saw me first and called after me to turn back; and some of my neighbors stood crying and calling after me to return. But I put my fingers in my ears and so came on my way."
Good-will: "But did none of them follow you, to persuade you to go back?"
Christian: "Yes, both Obstinate and Pliable; but when they saw they couldn't prevail, Obstinate went back grumbling, while Pliable came with me a little way."
Good-will: "But why did he not come through?"

Christian: "We did come together, until we reached the Slough of Despond, where we both suddenly fell in. Then my neighbor Pliable lost heart and would not go any further. So getting out again on the side nearest his own house, he told me I could have that fine country to myself; and he went his way, and I came mine — he after Obstinate, and I to this gate."
Good-will: Then Good-will said, "Alas, poor man! Is the heavenly glory of so little worth to him that he doesn't count it worth the risk of a few difficulties to obtain it?"

Christian: "Truly," said Christian, "I have told the truth about Pliable; and if I were to tell the whole truth about myself, you'd see there's no real difference between us. It's true he went back to his own house; but I also turned aside to walk the way of death, persuaded by the worldly arguments of one Mr. Worldly Wiseman."
Good-will: "Oh, did he get to you? What — he would have had you seek relief at the hands of Mr. Legality! They are both a thorough cheat. But did you take his advice?"
Christian: "Yes, as far as I dared. I went to find Mr. Legality, until I thought the mountain by his house would fall on my head; so there I was forced to stop."
Good-will: "That mountain has been the death of many, and will be the death of many more. It's well that you escaped being dashed to pieces by it."

Christian: "Truly, I don't know what would have become of me there, if Evangelist hadn't happily met me again while I stood there in my gloom. It was God's mercy that he came to me, or else I would never have come here. But now I am come — such as I am, more fit for death by that mountain than to stand talking with my lord. Yet oh, what a favor it is to me that I am allowed in here at all!"

Good-will: "We make no objection against anyone, no matter what they have done before they came here. They are in no way cast out. [John 6:37] So, good Christian, come a little way with me, and I will teach you about the way you must go. Look ahead of you — do you see this narrow way? That is the way you must go. It was laid out by the patriarchs, prophets, Christ, and his apostles, and it is as straight as a ruler can make it. This is the way you must go."
Christian: "But are there no turns or windings where a stranger might lose his way?"

Good-will: "Yes, there are many ways branching off from this one, and they are crooked and wide. But you can tell the right from the wrong this way: the right way is the only one that is straight and narrow." [Matt. 7:14]

Then I saw in my dream that Christian asked him further whether he could help him off with the burden on his back, for he had not yet been able to get rid of it, nor could he by any means get it off without help. Good-will told him, "As for your burden, be content to bear it until you come to the place of deliverance; for there it will fall from your back by itself."

Then Christian began to gird himself up and prepare for his journey. So Good-will told him that once he had gone some distance from the gate, he would come to the house of the Interpreter, where he should knock, and the Interpreter would show him excellent things. Then Christian took his leave of his friend, and Good-will again wished him Godspeed.
So he went on until he came to the house of the Interpreter, where he knocked again and again. At last someone came to the door and asked who was there.

Christian: "Sir, here is a traveler, told by an acquaintance of the master of this house to call here for my benefit; I would like to speak with the master." So the servant called for the master of the house, who, after a little while, came to Christian and asked what he wanted.

Christian: "Sir, I am a man come from the City of Destruction, on my way to Mount Zion; and I was told by the man who stands at the gate at the head of this way that if I called here, you would show me excellent things — things that would help me on my journey."

Interpreter: Then the Interpreter said, "Come in; I will show you what will be profitable to you." So he ordered his servant to light a candle, and told Christian to follow him; and he led him into a private room, and had his servant open a door. When he had done so, Christian saw the picture of a very solemn person hanging on the wall, and this was how it looked: it had eyes lifted up to heaven, the best of books in its hand, the law of truth written on its lips, and the world behind its back. It stood as if it were pleading with people, and a crown of gold hung over its head.
Christian: "What does this mean?"

Interpreter: "The man whose picture this is, is one in a thousand. He can father children [1 Cor. 4:15], labor in birth with children [Gal. 4:19], and nurse them himself once they are born. And whereas you see him with his eyes lifted to heaven, the best of books in his hand, and the law of truth on his lips, this is to show you that his work is to know and to unfold hidden things to sinners — just as you also see him standing as if pleading with people. And whereas you see the world cast behind him, and a crown hanging over his head, this is to show you that, because he scorns and despises the things of the present out of love for his Master's service, he is sure to have glory for his reward in the world to come. Now," said the Interpreter, "I have shown you this picture first because the man it portrays is the only one the Lord of the place you are going to has authorized to be your guide in all the difficult places you will meet on the way. So pay careful attention to what I have shown you, and keep it in mind, in case on your journey you meet some who pretend to lead you right, but whose way goes down to death."

Then he took him by the hand and led him into a very large parlor that was full of dust, because it was never swept. After Christian had looked at it a while, the Interpreter called for a man to sweep. Now when the man began to sweep, the dust flew about so thickly that Christian was almost choked by it. Then the Interpreter said to a young woman standing by, "Bring some water and sprinkle the room." When she had done so, it was swept and cleaned with ease.
Christian: "What does this mean?"

Interpreter: "This parlor is the heart of a man who was never made holy by the sweet grace of the gospel. The dust is his original sin and inward corruption, which have defiled the whole person. The one who began to sweep first is the Law; but the one who brought water and sprinkled it is the Gospel. Now, as you saw that as soon as the first began to sweep, the dust flew about so that the room could not be cleaned but you were almost choked by it — this is to show you that the Law, instead of cleansing the heart from sin, actually revives sin, gives it strength, and makes it grow in the soul, even as it uncovers and forbids it; for it gives no power to overcome it. [Rom. 7:6; 1 Cor. 15:56; Rom. 5:20] And as you saw the young woman sprinkle the room with water, so that it was cleaned with ease — this is to show you that when the gospel comes into the heart with its sweet and precious influences, then sin is conquered and subdued, and the soul is made clean through faith in it, and so made fit for the King of glory to live in." [John 15:3; Eph. 5:26; Acts 15:9]

Then I saw in my dream that the Interpreter took Christian by the hand and led him into a little room where two children sat, each in his own chair. The name of the older was Passion, and the name of the other Patience. Passion seemed very discontented, but Patience was very calm. Then Christian asked, "What is the reason for Passion's discontent?" The Interpreter answered, "Their Governor wants Passion to wait for his best things until the beginning of next year, but he will have them all now; whereas Patience is willing to wait."

Then I saw that someone came to Passion and brought him a bag of treasure and poured it out at his feet; and he took it up and rejoiced in it, and laughed Patience to scorn. But I watched only a little while, and he had squandered it all away, and had nothing left but rags.
Christian: Then Christian said to the Interpreter, "Explain this more fully to me."

Interpreter: "These two boys are figures. Passion stands for the men of this world, and Patience for the men of the world to come. For as you see, Passion will have everything now, this year — that is, in this world — and so it is with the men of this world: they must have all their good things now; they cannot wait until next year, that is, the next world, for their share of good. The proverb 'A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush' carries more weight with them than all the divine testimonies of the good of the world to come. But as you saw that Passion quickly squandered everything and was left with nothing but rags, so it will be with all such people at the end of this world."

Christian: "Now I see that Patience has the better wisdom, and that for many reasons: first, because he waits for the best things; and second, because he will have the glory of his when the other has nothing but rags."

Interpreter: "Indeed, and you may add another: the glory of the next world will never wear out, but these things are gone in a moment. So Passion had no more reason to laugh at Patience for having his good things first than Patience will have to laugh at Passion for having his best things last. For first must give place to last, because last must have its turn to come; but last gives place to nothing, for there is nothing to follow it. He, therefore, who has his portion first must spend it in time; but he who has his portion last has it lastingly. That is why it is said of the rich man, 'In your lifetime you received your good things, and likewise Lazarus evil things; but now he is comforted, and you are tormented.'" [Luke 16:25]
Christian: "Then I see it is not best to crave the things that are now, but to wait for the things to come."

Interpreter: "You speak the truth: 'For the things which are seen are temporary, but the things which are not seen are eternal.' [2 Cor. 4:18] Yet because things present and our fleshly appetite are such close neighbors, and because things to come and our worldly senses are such strangers to one another, that is why the first two so quickly strike up a friendship, and such a distance is kept between the others."

Then I saw in my dream that the Interpreter took Christian by the hand and led him to a place where a fire was burning against a wall, and someone stood by it constantly throwing water on it to put it out; yet the fire burned higher and hotter.
Christian: "What does this mean?"

Interpreter: "This fire is the work of grace at work in the heart. The one throwing water on it to quench it is the Devil. But to show you why the fire burns higher and hotter in spite of him, look here." So he led him around to the back of the wall, where Christian saw a man with a jar of oil in his hand, of which he continually but secretly threw some into the fire.
Christian: "What does this mean?"

Interpreter: "This is Christ, who continually, with the oil of his grace, sustains the work already begun in the heart; and by this means, in spite of all the Devil can do, the souls of his people remain full of grace. [2 Cor. 12:9] And as you saw that the man stood behind the wall to keep the fire going, that is to teach you how hard it is for the one being tempted to see how this work of grace is kept alive in the soul."

Then the Interpreter took him by the hand again and led him to a pleasant place where a stately and beautiful palace was built. At the sight of it Christian was greatly delighted. He also saw, on the top of it, certain people walking, all clothed in gold.
Christian: "May we go in there?"

Then the Interpreter led him up toward the door of the palace; and there at the door stood a great crowd of men who wanted to go in, but dared not. A little way off from the door sat a man at a table with a book and an inkwell before him, to record the name of anyone who would enter. Christian also saw that in the doorway stood many armored men to guard it, determined to do all the harm and mischief they could to anyone who tried to enter. Now Christian was somewhat amazed. At last, when every man drew back for fear of the armed men, Christian saw a man of very bold expression come up to the one who sat there to write, saying, "Set down my name, sir." When this was done, Christian saw the man draw his sword, put a helmet on his head, and rush toward the door at the armed men, who set on him with deadly force. But the man, not discouraged in the least, fell to cutting and hacking most fiercely. So after he had given and received many wounds, he cut his way through them all [Acts 14:22] and pressed forward into the palace, at which a pleasant voice was heard from those inside, even from those who walked on top of the palace, saying:
Come in, come in;
Eternal glory you shall win.
So he went in, and was clothed with garments like theirs. Then Christian smiled and said, "I think I truly understand the meaning of this."

Christian: "Now," said Christian, "let me go on." "No," said the Interpreter, "wait until I have shown you a little more, and after that you shall go on your way." So he took him by the hand again, and led him into a very dark room where a man sat in an iron cage.

Now the man looked very sad. He sat with his eyes fixed on the ground, his hands folded together, and he sighed as if his heart would break. Then Christian said, "What does this mean?" The Interpreter told him to talk with the man.
Then Christian said to the man, "Who are you?" The man answered, "I am what I once was not."
Christian: "What were you once?"

The man: "I was once a fine and flourishing professor of faith, both in my own eyes and in the eyes of others. [Luke 8:13] I once thought myself bound for the Celestial City, and I even had joy at the thought of getting there."
Christian: "Well, but what are you now?"
The man: "I am now a man of despair, and I am shut up in it as in this iron cage. I cannot get out. Oh, now I cannot!"
Christian: "But how did you come to this condition?"

The man: "I stopped watching and being sober. I gave free rein to my desires; I sinned against the light of the Word and the goodness of God. I have grieved the Spirit, and he is gone; I tempted the Devil, and he has come to me; I have provoked God to anger, and he has left me. I have so hardened my heart that I cannot repent."
Christian: Then Christian said to the Interpreter, "But is there no hope for such a man?" "Ask him," said the Interpreter. "No," said Christian, "please, sir, you ask him."
Interpreter: "Is there no hope? Must you be kept in this iron cage of despair?"
The man: "No, none at all."
Interpreter: "Why? The Son of the Blessed is very full of pity."

The man: "I have crucified him to myself afresh [Heb. 6:6]; I have despised his person [Luke 19:14]; I have despised his righteousness; I have counted his blood an unholy thing; I have done outrage to the Spirit of grace. [Heb. 10:28-29] So I have shut myself out of all the promises, and there now remains to me nothing but threats — dreadful, terrifying threats of certain judgment and fiery wrath that will devour me as an enemy."
Interpreter: "What brought you into this condition?"
The man: "The lusts, pleasures, and profits of this world; in enjoying them I promised myself much delight. But now every one of those very things bites and gnaws me like a burning worm."
Interpreter: "But can you not now repent and turn?"

The man: "God has denied me repentance. His Word gives me no encouragement to believe; in fact, he himself has shut me up in this iron cage, and not all the men in the world can let me out. O eternity, eternity! How shall I grapple with the misery I must meet in eternity!"
Interpreter: Then the Interpreter said to Christian, "Let this man's misery be remembered by you, and serve as an everlasting warning."
Christian: "Well," said Christian, "this is fearful! God help me to watch and be sober, and to pray that I may avoid the cause of this man's misery. Sir, isn't it time for me to go on my way now?"
Interpreter: "Wait until I show you one thing more, and then you shall go."

So he took Christian by the hand again and led him into a room where someone was getting out of bed; and as he put on his clothes, he shook and trembled. Then Christian asked, "Why does this man tremble so?" The Interpreter then asked the man to tell Christian the reason. So he began: "This night, as I slept, I dreamed, and the heavens grew exceedingly black. It also thundered and lightninged in the most fearful way, which threw me into agony. So in my dream I looked up and saw the clouds racing at an unusual speed, and I heard a great blast of a trumpet, and saw a man sitting on a cloud, attended by the thousands of heaven, all of them in flaming fire; and the heavens were ablaze. I then heard a voice saying, 'Arise, you dead, and come to judgment'; and with that the rocks split, the graves opened, and the dead who were in them came out. Some of them were exceedingly glad and looked upward; and some tried to hide themselves under the mountains. [1 Cor. 15:52; 1 Thes. 4:16; John 5:28,29] Then I saw the man who sat on the cloud open a book and command the world to draw near; yet, because of a fierce flame that came out from before him, there was a fitting distance kept between him and them, as between a judge and the prisoners at the bar. [Dan. 7:9,10] I heard it proclaimed to those attending the man on the cloud, 'Gather together the weeds, the chaff, and the stubble, and throw them into the burning lake.' [Matt. 13:30; Mal. 4:1] And with that, the bottomless pit opened, right about where I stood; and out of its mouth came smoke and coals of fire in abundance, with hideous noises. It was also said to the same attendants, 'Gather my wheat into the barn.' [Luke 3:17] And with that I saw many caught up and carried away into the clouds, but I was left behind. [1 Thes. 4:16,17] I also tried to hide myself, but I could not, for the man on the cloud kept his eye on me. My sins, too, came to mind, and my conscience accused me on every side. [Rom. 2:14,15] And with that I woke from my sleep."
Christian: "But what was it about this sight that made you so afraid?"

The man: "Why, I thought that the day of judgment had come and that I was not ready for it. But what frightened me most was that the angels gathered up several people and left me behind; and the pit of hell opened its mouth right where I stood. My conscience afflicted me, too; and, as I thought, the Judge always kept his eye on me, with indignation in his face."
Interpreter: Then the Interpreter said to Christian, "Have you considered all these things?"
Christian: "Yes, and they fill me with both hope and fear."

Interpreter: "Well, keep them all in your mind, so that they may be like a goad in your side, to spur you forward on the way you must go." Then Christian began to gird himself up and prepare for his journey. Then the Interpreter said, "May the Comforter always be with you, good Christian, to guide you in the way that leads to the City." So Christian went on his way, saying:
Here I have seen things rare and profitable;
Things pleasant, dreadful, things to make me stable
In what I have begun to take in hand;
Then let me think on them, and understand
Wherefore they showed me were, and let me be
Thankful, O good Interpreter, to thee.

Now I saw in my dream that the highway Christian was to travel was fenced on both sides with a wall, and that wall was called Salvation. [Isa. 26:1] Up this way, then, burdened Christian ran, but with great difficulty because of the load on his back.

He ran like this until he came to a place that rose a little, and on that place stood a cross, and a little below it, at the bottom, a tomb. So I saw in my dream that, just as Christian came up to the cross, his burden came loose from his shoulders, fell from his back, and began to tumble down, and so kept going until it came to the mouth of the tomb, where it fell in, and I saw it no more.

Then Christian was glad and light-hearted, and said with a merry heart, "He has given me rest by his sorrow, and life by his death." Then he stood still a while to look and wonder, for it was very surprising to him that the sight of the cross should so ease him of his burden. He looked, therefore, and looked again, until the springs in his head sent the water down his cheeks. [Zech. 12:10] Now, as he stood looking and weeping, three Shining Ones came to him and greeted him with "Peace be to you." So the first said to him, "Your sins are forgiven you" [Mark 2:5]; the second stripped him of his rags and clothed him with a change of clothing [Zech. 3:4]; the third also set a mark on his forehead and gave him a scroll with a seal on it, which he told him to look at as he ran, and to hand in at the Celestial Gate. [Eph. 1:13] So they went their way.
Who's this? The Pilgrim. How! 'Tis very true,
Old things are passed away, all's become new.
Strange! He's another man, upon my word;
They be fine feathers that make a fine bird.
Then Christian gave three leaps for joy, and went on singing:
Thus far I did come laden with my sin;
Nor could aught ease the grief that I was in
Till I came hither: what a place is this!
Must here be the beginning of my bliss?
Must here the burden fall from off my back?
Must here the strings that bound it to me crack?
Blest cross! Blest sepulchre! Blest rather be
The Man that there was put to shame for me!

I saw then in my dream that he went on until he came to a low place, where he saw, a little off the way, three men fast asleep with chains on their heels. The name of one was Simple, of another Sloth, and of the third Presumption.

Christian, seeing them lying like this, went to them in case he might wake them, and cried out, "You are like people sleeping on the top of a mast, for the Dead Sea is beneath you — a gulf that has no bottom. [Prov. 23:34] Wake up, then, and come away; be willing, and I will help you off with your chains." He also told them, "If the one who 'prowls about like a roaring lion' comes by, you will certainly be a prey to his teeth." [1 Pet. 5:8] At that they looked at him and began to reply, each in his way: Simple said, "I see no danger"; Sloth said, "Just a little more sleep"; and Presumption said, "Every tub must stand on its own bottom; what other answer should I give you?" And so they lay down to sleep again, and Christian went on his way.

Yet he was troubled to think that men in such danger should so little value the kindness of one who so freely offered to help them — by waking them, by counseling them, and by offering to help them off with their chains. And as he was troubled about this, he saw two men come tumbling over the wall on the left-hand side of the narrow way, and they hurried up to him. The name of one was Formalist, and the name of the other Hypocrisy. So, as I said, they came up to him, and he fell into conversation with them.
Christian: "Gentlemen, where have you come from, and where are you going?"
Formalist and Hypocrisy: "We were born in the land of Vainglory, and we are going for praise to Mount Zion."

Christian: "Why didn't you come in at the gate that stands at the beginning of the way? Don't you know it is written that whoever does not come in by the door, 'but climbs up some other way, the same is a thief and a robber'?" [John 10:1]

Formalist and Hypocrisy: They said that going to the gate for entry was, in the opinion of all their countrymen, too far around; and that their usual way was to make a shortcut of it and climb over the wall, as they had done.
Christian: "But won't it be counted a trespass against the Lord of the city we are bound for, to break his revealed will like that?"

Formalist and Hypocrisy: They told him that, as for that, he needn't trouble his head about it; for what they did, they had custom for, and could produce, if need be, testimony to support it going back more than a thousand years.
Christian: "But will your practice stand a trial at law?"

Formalist and Hypocrisy: They told him that custom, being of such long standing — over a thousand years — would surely now be accepted as legal by any impartial judge. "And besides," they said, "if we get into the way, what does it matter how we got in? If we're in, we're in. You are only in the way, having come in (as we see) at the gate; and we are also in the way, having come tumbling over the wall. How, then, is your condition any better than ours?"

Christian: "I walk by the rule of my Master; you walk by the rough working of your own fancies. You are counted thieves already by the Lord of the way; so I doubt you will be found true men at the end of it. You came in by yourselves, without his direction, and you will go out by yourselves, without his mercy."

To this they made him little answer, only telling him to look to himself. Then I saw that they each went on in their own way, with little conversation between them, except that the two men told Christian that, as for laws and ordinances, they had no doubt they would keep them as conscientiously as he. "So," they said, "we don't see how you differ from us, except by the coat on your back, which was (we suppose) given you by some of your neighbors to hide the shame of your nakedness."

Christian: "By laws and ordinances you will not be saved, since you did not come in by the door. [Gal. 2:16] And as for this coat on my back, it was given me by the Lord of the place I am going to — and, as you say, to cover my nakedness. I take it as a token of his kindness to me, for I had nothing but rags before. And besides, I comfort myself as I go like this: surely, I think, when I come to the gate of the city, the Lord of it will recognize me as good, since I have this coat on my back — a coat he gave me freely on the day he stripped me of my rags. I also have a mark on my forehead, which perhaps you have not noticed, set there by one of my Lord's closest companions on the day my burden fell off my shoulders. And what's more, I was then given a sealed scroll to comfort me by reading as I go, and was told to hand it in at the Celestial Gate as a token of my certain entry. I doubt you have any of these things — and you lack them because you did not come in at the gate."

To these things they gave him no answer; they only looked at each other and laughed. Then I saw that they all went on, except that Christian kept ahead, with no one to talk to but himself, sometimes sighing and sometimes comforted; and he would often read in the scroll one of the Shining Ones had given him, by which he was refreshed.

Then I saw that they all went on until they came to the foot of the Hill Difficulty, at the bottom of which was a spring. There were also, at the bottom of the hill, two other ways besides the one that came straight from the gate: one turned to the left, the other to the right. But the narrow way lay straight up the hill, and the name of the climb up the side of the hill is Difficulty. Christian now went to the spring and drank from it to refresh himself [Isa. 49:10], and then began to go up the hill, saying:
The hill, though high, I covet to ascend;
The difficulty will not me offend;
For I perceive the way to life lies here.
Come, pluck up heart, let's neither faint nor fear;
Better, though difficult, the right way to go,
Than wrong, though easy, where the end is woe.

The other two also came to the foot of the hill. But when they saw that the hill was steep and high, and that there were two other ways to go — and supposing that these two ways might meet up again with the one Christian took on the other side of the hill — they decided to take them. Now the name of one of these ways was Danger, and the name of the other Destruction. So the one took the way called Danger, which led him into a great wood; and the other took the way called Destruction, which led him into a wide field full of dark mountains, where he stumbled and fell, and rose no more.
Shall they who wrong begin yet rightly end?
Shall they at all have safety for their friend?
No, no; in headstrong manner they set out,
And headlong will they fall at last, no doubt.

Then I looked after Christian, to watch him go up the hill, where I saw him change from running to walking, and from walking to scrambling on his hands and knees, because the place was so steep. Now about halfway up the hill was a pleasant shelter, made by the Lord of the hill for the refreshment of weary travelers. There, then, Christian came, and sat down to rest. Then he pulled his scroll out of his coat and read in it to his comfort; he also took a fresh look at the coat that had been given him as he stood by the cross. Pleasing himself like this for a while, he at last fell into a doze, and then into a deep sleep, which kept him there until it was almost night; and as he slept, his scroll fell out of his hand. Now as he slept, someone came to him and woke him, saying, "Go to the ant, you sluggard; consider her ways and be wise." [Prov. 6:6] And with that Christian started up and hurried on his way, and went quickly until he came to the top of the hill.

Now when he reached the top, two men came running to meet him at full speed; the name of one was Timorous, and of the other Mistrust. Christian said to them, "Sirs, what's the matter? You're running the wrong way." Timorous answered that they had been going to the City of Zion and had climbed that difficult place; "but," he said, "the further we go, the more danger we meet; so we turned around and are going back."

"Yes," said Mistrust, "for just ahead of us there are a couple of lions in the way — whether asleep or awake we don't know — and we couldn't help thinking that if we came within reach, they would tear us to pieces at once."

Christian: Then Christian said, "You make me afraid; but where shall I flee to be safe? If I go back to my own country, which is prepared for fire and brimstone, I will certainly die there. If I can get to the Celestial City, I am sure to be safe. I must take the risk. To go back is nothing but death; to go forward is fear of death, with everlasting life beyond it. I will go forward still." So Mistrust and Timorous ran down the hill, and Christian went on his way. But, thinking again about what he had heard from the men, he felt in his coat for his scroll, so that he might read in it and be comforted; but he felt, and could not find it. Then Christian was in great distress, and did not know what to do; for he had lost the thing that usually comforted him, and that was to be his pass into the Celestial City. So he began to be greatly perplexed, and did not know what to do. At last he remembered that he had slept in the shelter on the side of the hill; and falling down on his knees, he asked God's forgiveness for that foolish act, and then went back to look for his scroll. But all the way back, who can describe the sorrow of Christian's heart? Sometimes he sighed, sometimes he wept, and often he scolded himself for being so foolish as to fall asleep in a place meant only for a little refreshment for his weariness. So he went back, carefully looking on this side and that all the way, in case he might find the scroll that had so often comforted him on his journey. He went on like this until he came again in sight of the shelter where he had sat and slept; but that sight only renewed his sorrow, by bringing his sin of sleeping fresh to mind. [Rev. 2:5; 1 Thes. 5:7,8] So he now went on lamenting his sinful sleep, saying, "O wretched man that I am, that I should sleep in the daytime! That I should sleep in the midst of difficulty! That I should so indulge the flesh as to use, for the ease of my flesh, the rest that the Lord of the hill set up only for the relief of pilgrims' spirits! How many steps have I taken in vain! This is what happened to Israel: for their sin, they were sent back by way of the Red Sea. And I am made to tread, with sorrow, the steps I might have trodden with delight, if it hadn't been for this sinful sleep. How far might I have been on my way by now! I am made to walk three times over the ground I needed to walk only once; and now I am likely to be caught by nightfall, too, for the day is almost spent. Oh, that I had not slept!"

Now by this time he had come back to the shelter, where he sat down for a while and wept. But at last, as Christian would have it, looking sorrowfully down under the bench, he spotted his scroll. With trembling and haste he snatched it up and put it back inside his coat. But who can tell how joyful this man was when he had gotten his scroll again? For this scroll was the assurance of his life and his acceptance at the longed-for haven. So he tucked it into his coat, gave thanks to God for directing his eye to the place where it lay, and with joy and tears set out again on his journey. But oh, how nimbly he now went up the rest of the hill! Yet before he reached the top, the sun went down on Christian; and this again reminded him of the foolishness of his sleeping, so that he again began to lament: "O sinful sleep! Because of you I am likely to be overtaken by night on my journey. I must walk without the sun; darkness must cover my path; and I must hear the noise of the doleful creatures, all because of my sinful sleep." [1 Thes. 5:6,7] Now he also remembered the story Mistrust and Timorous had told him, of how they were frightened by the sight of the lions. Then Christian said to himself again, "These beasts roam at night for their prey; if they should meet me in the dark, how could I escape them? How could I avoid being torn to pieces by them?" So he went on his way. But while he was lamenting his unhappy misfortune, he lifted up his eyes, and there before him was a very stately palace, the name of which was Beautiful, and it stood right beside the highway.

So I saw in my dream that he hurried forward, hoping he might get lodging there. Now before he had gone far, he came into a very narrow passage, about a hundred yards from the porter's lodge; and looking very carefully ahead as he went, he spotted two lions in the way. "Now," he thought, "I see the dangers that drove Mistrust and Timorous back." (The lions were chained, but he did not see the chains.) Then he was afraid, and thought of going back too, for he thought nothing but death was ahead of him. But the porter at the lodge, whose name is Watchful, seeing that Christian had stopped as if to turn back, called out to him, "Is your strength so small? [Mark 8:34-37] Don't be afraid of the lions, for they are chained, and are placed there to test faith where it exists, and to expose those who have none. Keep to the middle of the path, and no harm will come to you."
Difficulty is behind, Fear is before,
Though he's got on the hill, the lions roar;
A Christian man is never long at ease,
When one fright's gone, another doth him seize.

Then I saw that he went on, trembling for fear of the lions, but taking good heed to the porter's directions; he heard them roar, but they did him no harm. Then he clapped his hands and went on until he came and stood before the gate where the porter was. Then Christian said to the porter, "Sir, what house is this? And may I lodge here tonight?" The porter answered, "This house was built by the Lord of the hill, and he built it for the relief and safety of pilgrims." The porter also asked where he was from and where he was going.
Christian: "I have come from the City of Destruction, and am going to Mount Zion; but because the sun has now set, I would like, if I may, to lodge here tonight."
Porter: "What is your name?"
Christian: "My name is now Christian, but at first my name was Graceless. I come from the line of Japheth, whom God will persuade to dwell in the tents of Shem." [Gen. 9:27]
Porter: "But how is it that you come so late? The sun has set."

Christian: "I would have been here sooner, but — wretched man that I am! — I slept in the shelter on the hillside. Even so, I would have been here much sooner, but in my sleep I lost my proof, and came without it to the brow of the hill; and then, feeling for it and not finding it, I was forced, with sorrow of heart, to go back to the place where I slept, where I found it; and now I am here."

Porter: "Well, I will call out one of the young women of this place, who, if she likes your conversation, will bring you in to the rest of the household, according to the rules of the house." So Watchful the porter rang a bell, and at the sound there came out at the door of the house a solemn and beautiful young woman named Discretion, who asked why she had been called.

The porter answered, "This man is on a journey from the City of Destruction to Mount Zion, but being weary and overtaken by night, he asked me if he might lodge here tonight. So I told him I would call for you, who, after speaking with him, may do as you think best, according to the law of the house."

Then she asked him where he was from and where he was going, and he told her. She also asked how he had gotten into the way, and he told her. Then she asked what he had seen and met with on the way, and he told her. And last she asked his name; so he said, "It is Christian, and I have all the more a desire to lodge here tonight, because, as I understand, this place was built by the Lord of the hill for the relief and safety of pilgrims." So she smiled, but the tears stood in her eyes; and after a little pause she said, "I will call out two or three more of the household." So she ran to the door and called out Prudence, Piety, and Charity, who, after a little more conversation with him, brought him into the household; and many of them, meeting him at the threshold of the house, said, "Come in, you blessed of the Lord; this house was built by the Lord of the hill on purpose to welcome such pilgrims as you." Then he bowed his head and followed them into the house. So when he had come in and sat down, they gave him something to drink, and agreed together that, until supper was ready, some of them should have a particular conversation with Christian, to make the best use of the time; and they appointed Piety, Prudence, and Charity to talk with him; and so they began.

Piety: "Come, good Christian, since we have been so loving to you as to welcome you into our house tonight, let us, if perhaps we may better ourselves by it, talk with you about everything that has happened to you on your pilgrimage."
Christian: "With a very good will; and I am glad you are so kindly disposed."
Piety: "What first moved you to take up a pilgrim's life?"
Christian: "I was driven out of my native country by a dreadful sound that kept ringing in my ears: namely, that unavoidable destruction awaited me if I stayed where I was."
Piety: "But how did it come about that you left your country this way?"

Christian: "It was as God would have it; for when I was under the fear of destruction, I did not know where to go. But as I was trembling and weeping, a man named Evangelist happened to come to me, and he directed me to the wicket-gate, which I would otherwise never have found, and so set me on the way that has led me straight to this house."
Piety: "But did you not come by the house of the Interpreter?"

Christian: "Yes, and I saw such things there that I will remember as long as I live — especially three things: how Christ, in spite of Satan, keeps up his work of grace in the heart; how a man had sinned himself right out of all hope of God's mercy; and the dream of the man who thought in his sleep that the day of judgment had come."
Piety: "Why, did you hear him tell his dream?"
Christian: "Yes, and a dreadful one it was. It made my heart ache as he told it; yet I am glad I heard it."
Piety: "Was that all you saw at the house of the Interpreter?"

Christian: "No; he took me where he showed me a stately palace, and how the people in it were clothed in gold; and how a daring man cut his way through the armed men at the door who tried to keep him out, and how he was told to come in and win eternal glory. Those things did ravish my heart! I would have stayed at that good man's house a whole year, except that I knew I had further to go."
Piety: "And what else did you see on the way?"

Christian: "See! Why, I had gone only a little further when I saw one, as I thought in my mind, hanging and bleeding on a tree; and the very sight of him made my burden fall off my back (for I was groaning under a very heavy burden), and there it fell from me. It was a strange thing to me, for I had never seen such a thing before. And while I stood looking up — for then I could not stop looking — three Shining Ones came to me. One of them testified that my sins were forgiven me; another stripped me of my rags and gave me this embroidered coat you see; and the third set the mark you see on my forehead, and gave me this sealed scroll." (And with that he pulled it out of his coat.)
Piety: "But you saw more than this, didn't you?"

Christian: "The things I have told you were the best; yet I saw some other things too: I saw three men, Simple, Sloth, and Presumption, lying asleep a little off the way as I came, with chains on their heels — but do you think I could wake them? I also saw Formalist and Hypocrisy come tumbling over the wall to go, as they pretended, to Zion; but they were quickly lost, just as I told them they would be, though they would not believe me. But above all, I found it hard work to get up this hill, and just as hard to come by the lions' mouths; and truly, if it hadn't been for the good porter who stands at the gate, I don't know but that I might have gone back after all. But now I thank God I am here, and I thank you for receiving me."
Then Prudence thought it good to ask him a few questions, and asked for his answers to them.
Prudence: "Do you not sometimes think of the country you came from?"
Christian: "Yes, but with much shame and loathing. Truly, if I had kept that country in mind, I might have had a chance to go back; but now I desire a better country, a heavenly one." [Heb. 11:15,16]
Prudence: "Do you not still carry with you some of the things you were involved with then?"

Christian: "Yes, but greatly against my will; especially my inward and worldly thoughts, which all my countrymen, as well as myself, delighted in. But now all those things are my grief; and if I could choose for myself, I would choose never to think of them again. But when I want to do what is best, what is worst is right there with me." [Rom. 7:16-19]
Prudence: "Do you not sometimes find that those things seem conquered, which at other times are your torment?"
Christian: "Yes, but only seldom; those are golden hours to me, when such things happen."
Prudence: "Can you remember by what means you find your troubles seeming, at times, to be conquered?"

Christian: "Yes: when I think of what I saw at the cross, that will do it; and when I look at my embroidered coat, that will do it; and when I look into the scroll I carry in my coat, that will do it; and when my thoughts grow warm about where I am going, that will do it."
Prudence: "And what is it that makes you so eager to go to Mount Zion?"

Christian: "Why, there I hope to see alive the one who hung dead on the cross; and there I hope to be rid of all the things that to this day are an annoyance in me. There, they say, there is no death; and there I will live with the company I like best. [Isa. 25:8; Rev. 21:4] For, to tell you the truth, I love him because by him I was eased of my burden; and I am weary of my inward sickness. I would gladly be where I shall die no more, and with the company that will continually cry, 'Holy, Holy, Holy!'"
Then Charity said to Christian, "Do you have a family? Are you a married man?"
Christian: "I have a wife and four small children."
Charity: "And why did you not bring them along with you?"
Christian: Then Christian wept and said, "Oh, how gladly I would have done it! But they were all utterly opposed to my going on pilgrimage."
Charity: "But you should have talked to them, and tried to show them the danger of staying behind."
Christian: "I did; and I also told them what God had shown me about the destruction of our city. But I seemed to them like one who mocked, and they did not believe me." [Gen. 19:14]
Charity: "And did you pray to God that he would bless your counsel to them?"
Christian: "Yes, and with much affection; for you must understand that my wife and poor children were very dear to me."
Charity: "But did you tell them of your own sorrow and fear of destruction? For I suppose that destruction was visible enough to you."

Christian: "Yes, over and over and over again. They could also see my fear in my face, in my tears, and in my trembling under the dread of the judgment hanging over our heads. But none of it was enough to persuade them to come with me."
Charity: "But what could they say for themselves, as to why they would not come?"

Christian: "Why, my wife was afraid of losing this world, and my children were given over to the foolish pleasures of youth. So, what by one thing and what by another, they left me to wander like this alone."
Charity: "But did you not, by your own empty life, undermine all the persuading you did with words to bring them away with you?"

Christian: "Indeed, I cannot commend my life, for I am conscious of many failings in it. I know too that a man may, by his conduct, quickly overthrow what he labors by argument or persuasion to fasten on others for their good. Yet I can say this: I was very careful not to give them any reason, by some unseemly action, to be put off going on pilgrimage. In fact, for this very thing they would tell me I was too strict, and that I denied myself things, for their sakes, in which they saw no evil. No — I think I may say that if what they saw in me hindered them, it was my great carefulness not to sin against God or do any wrong to my neighbor."

Charity: "Indeed, Cain hated his brother because 'his own works were evil, and his brother's righteous' [1 John 3:12]; and if your wife and children have been offended with you for this, they thereby show themselves to be set against good, and 'you have delivered your soul from their blood.'" [Ezek. 3:19]

Now I saw in my dream that they sat talking together like this until supper was ready. So when it was prepared, they sat down to eat. Now the table was furnished with rich food and well-refined wine; and all their talk at the table was about the Lord of the hill — namely, what he had done, and why he did what he did, and why he had built that house. And by what they said, I gathered that he had been a great warrior, and had fought with and slain him who had the power of death, but not without great danger to himself, which made me love him the more. [Heb. 2:14,15]

For, as they said, and as I believe (said Christian), he did it with the loss of much blood; but what put a glory of grace into all he did was that he did it out of pure love for his country.
