And besides, there were some of the household who said they had been with him and spoken with him since he died on the cross; and they testified that they had it from his own lips that he is such a lover of poor pilgrims that the like is not to be found from the east to the west.

They also gave an example of what they claimed, namely, that he had stripped himself of his glory so that he might do this for the poor; and that they had heard him say and affirm that he would not dwell on the mountain of Zion alone. They said, moreover, that he had made many pilgrims into princes, though by nature they were born beggars, and their origin had been the dunghill. [1 Sam. 2:8; Ps. 113:7]

So they talked together like this until late at night; and after they had committed themselves to their Lord for protection, they took their rest. They laid the Pilgrim in a large upper room whose window opened toward the sunrise; the name of the room was Peace, and there he slept until daybreak, and then he woke and sang:
Where am I now? Is this the love and care
Of Jesus for the men that pilgrims are?
Thus to provide! That I should be forgiven!
And dwell already the next door to heaven!

So in the morning they all got up; and, after some more conversation, they told him that he should not leave until they had shown him the rare things of that place. First they took him into the study, where they showed him records of the greatest antiquity. In these, as I remember my dream, they showed him first the pedigree of the Lord of the hill: that he was the Son of the Ancient of Days, and came by that eternal generation. Here too was more fully recorded the deeds he had done, and the names of many hundreds he had taken into his service, and how he had placed them in dwellings that neither length of days nor decay of nature could dissolve.

Then they read to him some of the worthy deeds that some of his servants had done: how they had "subdued kingdoms, worked righteousness, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions, quenched the violence of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, out of weakness were made strong, grew valiant in battle, and turned to flight the armies of foreigners." [Heb. 11:33,34]

Then they read again, in another part of the records of the house, where it was shown how willing their Lord was to receive into his favor anyone — anyone at all — even those who in times past had offered great insults to his person and his proceedings. Here too were several other histories of many famous things, all of which Christian saw: things both ancient and modern, together with prophecies and predictions of things that will certainly come to pass, both to the dread and amazement of his enemies and the comfort and solace of pilgrims.

The next day they took him into the armory, where they showed him all kinds of equipment that their Lord had provided for pilgrims: sword, shield, helmet, breastplate, all-prayer, and shoes that would not wear out. And there was enough here to equip as many men for the service of their Lord as there are stars in the sky for number.

They also showed him some of the instruments with which some of his servants had done wonderful things. They showed him Moses' rod; the hammer and nail with which Jael killed Sisera; the pitchers, trumpets, and lamps with which Gideon put to flight the armies of Midian. Then they showed him the ox-goad with which Shamgar killed six hundred men. They also showed him the jawbone with which Samson did such mighty feats. They showed him, moreover, the sling and the stone with which David killed Goliath of Gath; and the sword, too, with which their Lord will kill the Man of Sin in the day that he rises up to the prey. They showed him besides many excellent things, with which Christian was much delighted. This done, they went to their rest again.

Then I saw in my dream that the next morning he got up to go forward, but they asked him to stay until the next day as well. "And then," they said, "if the day is clear, we will show you the Delectable Mountains, which will further add to your comfort, because they are nearer the longed-for haven than the place where you are now." So he agreed and stayed. When morning had come, they took him to the top of the house and told him to look south; so he did, and behold, at a great distance he saw a most pleasant, mountainous country, beautiful with woods, vineyards, fruits of all sorts, flowers too, with springs and fountains, very delightful to behold. [Isa. 33:16,17] Then he asked the name of the country. They said it was Immanuel's Land; "and it is as much for all the pilgrims," they said, "as this hill is. And when you come there, you will be able to see the gate of the Celestial City, as the shepherds who live there will show you."

Now he thought of setting out, and they were willing he should. "But first," they said, "let us go again to the armory." So they did; and when they came there, they equipped him from head to foot with armor that would hold, in case he should meet with assaults along the way. So, thus outfitted, he walked out with his friends to the gate; and there he asked the porter whether he had seen any pilgrims pass by. The porter answered, "Yes."
Christian: "Please, did you know him?"
Porter: "I asked him his name, and he told me it was Faithful."
Christian: "Oh," said Christian, "I know him; he is my townsman, my near neighbor; he comes from the place where I was born. How far ahead do you think he might be?"
Porter: "He has gotten by this time below the hill."
Christian: "Well, good porter, the Lord be with you, and add much increase to all your blessings, for the kindness you have shown me."

Then he began to go forward; but Discretion, Piety, Charity, and Prudence wanted to accompany him down to the foot of the hill. So they went on together, going over their earlier conversations, until they came to begin the descent. Then Christian said, "As it was difficult coming up, so, as far as I can see, it is dangerous going down." "Yes," said Prudence, "so it is; for it is a hard thing for a man to go down into the Valley of Humiliation, as you are about to do, without catching a slip on the way. That is why we have come out to accompany you down the hill." So he began to go down, but very carefully; yet even so, he caught a slip or two.

Then I saw in my dream that these good companions, when Christian had reached the bottom of the hill, gave him a loaf of bread, a bottle of wine, and a cluster of raisins; and then he went on his way.

But now, in this Valley of Humiliation, poor Christian was hard pressed; for he had gone only a little way when he saw a foul fiend coming over the field to meet him; his name is Apollyon. Then Christian began to be afraid, and to turn over in his mind whether to go back or to stand his ground. But he considered that he had no armor for his back, and so thought that to turn his back might give the fiend a greater advantage, letting him pierce him easily with his darts. So he resolved to take the risk and stand his ground; "for," he thought, "if I had nothing in view but the saving of my life, it would still be best to stand."

So he went on, and Apollyon met him. Now the monster was hideous to behold: he was clothed with scales like a fish (and these are his pride); he had wings like a dragon, feet like a bear, and out of his belly came fire and smoke; and his mouth was like the mouth of a lion. When he had come up to Christian, he looked at him with a disdainful expression, and began to question him.
Apollyon: "Where have you come from, and where are you bound?"
Christian: "I have come from the City of Destruction, which is the place of all evil, and I am going to the City of Zion."

Apollyon: "By this I see that you are one of my subjects, for all that country is mine, and I am the prince and god of it. How is it, then, that you have run away from your king? If I did not hope you might yet do me more service, I would strike you down to the ground at one blow."

Christian: "I was indeed born in your dominions, but your service was hard, and your wages were such that a man could not live on them; 'for the wages of sin is death.' [Rom. 6:23] So when I came of age, I did as other thoughtful people do, and looked around to see if perhaps I might better myself."

Apollyon: "No prince will lightly lose his subjects like this, and neither will I lose you yet. But since you complain about your service and wages, be content to go back, and what our country can offer, I here promise to give you."
Christian: "But I have bound myself to another, even to the King of princes; and how can I, in fairness, go back with you?"

Apollyon: "You have done, in this, according to the proverb: 'Changed a bad for a worse.' But it is common for those who have professed themselves his servants, after a while, to give him the slip and return to me. Do the same, and all will be well."
Christian: "I have given him my faith and sworn my allegiance to him; how, then, can I go back from this and not be hanged as a traitor?"
Apollyon: "You did the same to me, and yet I am willing to overlook it all, if you will only turn again and go back now."

Christian: "What I promised you was when I was too young to know better; and besides, I count that the Prince under whose banner I now stand is able to absolve me — yes, and to pardon what I did in going along with you. And besides, O destroying Apollyon, to tell the truth, I like his service, his wages, his servants, his government, his company, and his country better than yours. So stop trying to persuade me further; I am his servant, and I will follow him."

Apollyon: "Consider again, in cool blood, what you are likely to meet with on the way you are going. You know that, for the most part, his servants come to a bad end, because they are transgressors against me and my ways. How many of them have been put to shameful deaths! And besides, you count his service better than mine, whereas he has never yet come from the place where he is to deliver any who served him out of the hands of their enemies. But as for me, how many times — as all the world well knows — have I delivered, either by power or by fraud, those who have faithfully served me, even when they were captured by him and his; and so I will deliver you."

Christian: "His refraining, for the present, to deliver them is on purpose, to test their love, to see whether they will cleave to him to the end. And as for the bad end you say they come to, that is most glorious in their account; for as for present deliverance, they do not much expect it, for they wait for their glory, and then they will have it, when their Prince comes in his glory and the glory of the angels."
Apollyon: "You have already been unfaithful in your service to him; so how do you think to receive wages from him?"
Christian: "In what way, O Apollyon, have I been unfaithful to him?"

Apollyon: "You fainted at the very first setting out, when you were almost choked in the Gulf of Despond. You tried wrong ways to be rid of your burden, when you should have waited until your Prince had taken it off. You sinfully fell asleep and lost your precious thing. You were also almost persuaded to go back at the sight of the lions. And when you talk of your journey, and of what you have heard and seen, you are inwardly desirous of vainglory in all that you say or do."

Christian: "All this is true, and much more besides that you have left out. But the Prince whom I serve and honor is merciful and ready to forgive. Besides, these weaknesses took hold of me in your country, for there I drank them in; and I have groaned under them, been sorry for them, and have obtained pardon from my Prince."
Apollyon: Then Apollyon broke out into a terrible rage, saying, "I am an enemy to this Prince; I hate his person, his laws, and his people; I have come out on purpose to withstand you."
Christian: "Apollyon, beware what you do; for I am in the King's highway, the way of holiness; so watch yourself."

Apollyon: Then Apollyon straddled across the whole width of the way, and said, "I have no fear in this matter. Prepare to die; for I swear by my infernal den that you shall go no further; here I will spill your soul."
And with that he threw a flaming dart at his breast; but Christian had a shield in his hand, with which he caught it, and so avoided the danger of it.

Then Christian drew his sword, for he saw it was time to bestir himself; and Apollyon came at him just as fast, throwing darts as thick as hail. By these, despite all Christian could do to avoid it, Apollyon wounded him in his head, his hand, and his foot. This made Christian give a little ground; so Apollyon pressed his attack with all his might, and Christian again took courage and resisted as manfully as he could. This grievous combat lasted more than half a day, until Christian was almost completely spent; for you must understand that Christian, by reason of his wounds, grew weaker and weaker.

Then Apollyon, seeing his chance, began to close in on Christian, and wrestling with him, gave him a dreadful fall; and with that Christian's sword flew out of his hand. Then Apollyon said, "I am sure of you now." And with that he almost pressed him to death, so that Christian began to despair of life. But as God would have it, while Apollyon was fetching his last blow, to make a full end of this good man, Christian nimbly reached out his hand for his sword and caught it, saying, "Rejoice not against me, O my enemy; when I fall, I shall arise" [Micah 7:8]; and with that he gave him a deadly thrust, which made Apollyon give back, as one who had received a mortal wound. Christian, seeing that, made at him again, saying, "No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us." [Rom. 8:37] And with that Apollyon spread out his dragon's wings and sped away, so that Christian saw him no more for a time. [James 4:7]

In this combat, no one can imagine — unless he had seen and heard it, as I did — what yelling and hideous roaring Apollyon made the whole time of the fight; he spoke like a dragon. And on the other side, what sighs and groans burst from Christian's heart! I never saw him give so much as one pleasant look the whole time, until he saw that he had wounded Apollyon with his two-edged sword; then indeed he did smile and look upward; but it was the most dreadful sight I ever saw.
A more unequal match can hardly be —
Christian must fight an angel; but you see,
The valiant man, by handling sword and shield,
Doth make him, though a dragon, quit the field.
So when the battle was over, Christian said, "I will here give thanks to him who delivered me out of the mouth of the lion, to him who helped me against Apollyon." And so he did, saying:
Great Beelzebub, the captain of this fiend,
Designed my ruin; therefore to this end
He sent him harnessed out; and he with rage
That hellish was, did fiercely me engage.
But blessed Michael helped me, and I,
By dint of sword, did quickly make him fly.
Therefore to him let me give lasting praise,
And thank and bless his holy name always.

Then there came to him a hand holding some of the leaves of the tree of life, which Christian took and applied to the wounds he had received in the battle, and he was healed immediately. He also sat down in that place to eat bread and to drink from the bottle that had been given him a little before; and so, being refreshed, he set out again on his journey with his sword drawn in his hand; "for," he said, "I don't know but some other enemy may be at hand." But he met with no other assault from Apollyon all through this valley.

Now at the end of this valley was another, called the Valley of the Shadow of Death; and Christian had to go through it, because the way to the Celestial City lay through the middle of it. Now this valley is a very lonely place. The prophet Jeremiah describes it like this: "A wilderness, a land of deserts and of pits, a land of drought and of the shadow of death, a land that no one" (but a Christian) "passes through, and where no one lives." [Jer. 2:6]
Here Christian was worse put to it than in his fight with Apollyon, as you will see by what follows.

I saw then in my dream that when Christian had come to the borders of the Shadow of Death, two men met him — sons of those who had brought back an evil report of the good land [Num. 13] — hurrying to go back. Christian spoke to them as follows:
Christian: "Where are you going?"
The men: "Back! Back! And we would have you do the same, if you value either life or peace."
Christian: "Why, what's the matter?"

The men: "Matter! We were going that way you are going, and went as far as we dared; and indeed we were almost past coming back; for had we gone a little further, we would not be here to bring you the news."
Christian: "But what have you met with?"
The men: "Why, we were almost in the Valley of the Shadow of Death; but by good fortune we looked ahead and saw the danger before we came to it." [Ps. 44:19; 107:10]
Christian: "But what have you seen?"

The men: "Seen! Why, the Valley itself, which is as dark as pitch; we also saw there the hobgoblins, satyrs, and dragons of the pit. We also heard in that Valley a continual howling and yelling, like a people in unutterable misery, sitting there bound in affliction and chains; and over that Valley hang the discouraging clouds of confusion. Death also always spreads his wings over it. In a word, it is every bit dreadful, being utterly without order." [Job 3:5; 10:22]
Christian: "Then," said Christian, "from what you have said, I still see nothing but that this is my way to the longed-for haven." [Jer. 2:6]
The men: "Be it your way; we will not choose it for ours." So they parted, and Christian went on his way, but still with his sword drawn in his hand, for fear he should be assaulted.

I saw then in my dream that, as far as this valley reached, there was on the right hand a very deep ditch — the ditch into which the blind have led the blind in all ages, and where both have miserably perished. [Ps. 69:14,15] And again, on the left hand, there was a very dangerous bog, into which, if even a good man falls, he can find no bottom for his foot to stand on. Into that bog King David once fell, and would no doubt have been smothered in it, if he who is able had not plucked him out.

The path here was also exceedingly narrow, and so good Christian was the more hard pressed; for when he tried, in the dark, to avoid the ditch on the one side, he was ready to tip over into the mire on the other; and when he tried to escape the mire, without great care he would be ready to fall into the ditch. So he went on, and I heard him sigh bitterly; for, besides the dangers I mentioned, the path here was so dark that often, when he lifted his foot to step forward, he did not know where or on what he should set it next.
Poor man! Where art thou now? Thy day is night.
Good man, be not cast down, thou yet art right;
Thy way to heaven lies by the gates of hell;
Cheer up, hold out, with thee it shall go well.

About the middle of this valley, I saw the mouth of hell, and it stood close by the wayside. "Now," thought Christian, "what shall I do?" And every now and then the flame and smoke would come out in such abundance, with sparks and hideous noises (things that cared nothing for Christian's sword, as Apollyon had before), that he was forced to put up his sword and take up another weapon called All-prayer. [Eph. 6:18] So he cried out, in my hearing, "O Lord, I beg you, deliver my soul!" [Ps. 116:4] So he went on a great while, yet still the flames kept reaching toward him. He also heard mournful voices, and rushings to and fro, so that sometimes he thought he would be torn to pieces or trodden down like mud in the streets. This frightful sight, and these dreadful noises, he saw and heard for several miles together; and coming to a place where he thought he heard a company of fiends coming forward to meet him, he stopped and began to consider what was best to do. Sometimes he had half a mind to go back; then again he thought he might be halfway through the valley. He remembered too how he had already overcome many a danger, and that the danger of going back might be much greater than going forward; so he resolved to go on. Yet the fiends seemed to come nearer and nearer; but when they were come almost up to him, he cried out with a most forceful voice, "I will walk in the strength of the Lord God!" — and at that they gave back, and came no further.

One thing I must not leave out: I noticed that now poor Christian was so bewildered that he did not know his own voice; and this is how I perceived it. Just when he had come opposite the mouth of the burning pit, one of the wicked ones got behind him, and stepped up softly to him, and whisperingly suggested many grievous blasphemies to him, which he truly thought had come from his own mind. This put Christian more to it than anything he had met with before — even to think that he should now blaspheme the one he had loved so much before. Yet if he could have helped it, he would not have done it; but he did not have the presence of mind either to stop his ears or to recognize where these blasphemies came from.

When Christian had traveled in this dismal condition for a considerable time, he thought he heard the voice of a man, going on ahead of him, saying, "Though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me." [Ps. 23:4]

Then he was glad, and for these reasons: first, because he gathered from it that some who feared God were in this valley as well as himself; second, because he saw that God was with them, even in that dark and dismal state — "and why not," he thought, "with me, though because of the difficulties of this place I cannot perceive it?" [Job 9:11]; third, because he hoped that, if he could overtake them, he would have company by and by. So he went on, and called to the one ahead of him; but that man did not know what to answer, for he too thought himself alone. And by and by the day broke; then Christian said, "He has turned the shadow of death into the morning." [Amos 5:8]

Now that morning had come, he looked back — not out of any desire to go back, but to see, by the light of day, what hazards he had come through in the dark. So he saw more clearly the ditch on the one side and the mire on the other; also how narrow the way was that led between them both. Now too he saw the hobgoblins, and satyrs, and dragons of the pit, but all far off (for after daybreak they did not come near); yet they were revealed to him, according to what is written: "He uncovers deep things out of darkness, and brings out to light the shadow of death." [Job 12:22]

Now Christian was much moved by his deliverance from all the dangers of his lonely way — dangers which, though he had feared them more before, he now saw more clearly, because the daylight made them plain to him. And about this time the sun was rising; and this was another mercy to Christian, for you must note that, though the first part of the Valley of the Shadow of Death was dangerous, the second part, which he had yet to go, was, if possible, far more dangerous. For from the place where he now stood, all the way to the end of the valley, the way was so full of snares, traps, gins, and nets here, and so full of pits, pitfalls, deep holes, and steep drops there, that if it had been as dark as when he came through the first part, he might have had a thousand souls and reasonably lost them all. But, as I said, the sun was rising. Then he said, "His candle shines on my head, and by his light I walk through darkness." [Job 29:3]

In this light, then, he came to the end of the valley. Now I saw in my dream that at the end of this valley lay blood, bones, ashes, and mangled bodies of men, even of pilgrims who had gone this way before. And while I was wondering what the reason might be, I spotted a little ahead of me a cave, where two giants, Pope and Pagan, had lived in old times; by whose power and tyranny the men whose bones, blood, and ashes lay there had been cruelly put to death. But Christian went past this place without much danger, which I somewhat wondered at. But I have learned since that Pagan has been dead many a day; and as for the other, though he is still alive, he is, by reason of age, and also of the many shrewd batterings he met with in his younger days, grown so stiff in his joints that he can now do little more than sit in his cave's mouth, grinning at pilgrims as they go by, and biting his nails because he cannot get at them.

So I saw that Christian went on his way; yet, at the sight of the old man who sat in the mouth of the cave, he could not tell what to think — especially because the old man spoke to him, though he could not get up to go after him, saying, "You will never mend till more of you be burned." But Christian held his peace, set a good face on it, and so went by and caught no harm. Then Christian sang:
O world of wonders! (I can say no less),
That I should be preserved in that distress
That I have met with here! O blessed be
That hand that from it hath delivered me!
Dangers in darkness, devils, hell, and sin
Did compass me, while I this vale was in:
Yea, snares, and pits, and traps, and nets, did lie
My path about, that worthless, silly I
Might have been catched, entangled, and cast down;
But since I live, let Jesus wear the crown.

Now, as Christian went on his way, he came to a little rise, which had been thrown up on purpose so that pilgrims might see ahead of them. Up there, then, Christian went, and looking forward, he saw Faithful ahead of him on his journey. Then Christian called out aloud, "Hey! Hey! Hold on, and I will be your companion!" At that, Faithful looked behind him; to whom Christian cried again, "Wait, wait, until I come up to you!" But Faithful answered, "No, I am running for my life, and the avenger of blood is behind me."

At this Christian was somewhat stirred, and putting out all his strength, he quickly caught up with Faithful, and even ran past him; so the last became first. Then Christian smiled with a touch of vainglory, because he had gotten ahead of his brother; but not watching his feet, he suddenly stumbled and fell, and could not get up again until Faithful came to help him.
Then I saw in my dream that they went on very lovingly together, and had sweet conversation about all the things that had happened to them on their pilgrimage; and so Christian began:
Christian: "My honored and well-beloved brother Faithful, I am glad I have overtaken you, and that God has so tempered our spirits that we can walk as companions on this pleasant path."
Faithful: "Dear friend, I had thought to have your company all the way from our town; but you got the start of me, so I was forced to come this much of the way alone."
Christian: "How long did you stay in the City of Destruction before you set out after me on your pilgrimage?"
Faithful: "Until I could stay no longer; for there was great talk, soon after you left, that our city would shortly be burned to the ground with fire from heaven."
Christian: "What! Did your neighbors talk like that?"
Faithful: "Yes, it was for a while in everybody's mouth."
Christian: "What! And did no more of them but you come out to escape the danger?"

Faithful: "Though there was, as I said, great talk about it, I don't think they firmly believed it. For in the heat of the talk I heard some of them speak mockingly of you and of your desperate journey, as they called this pilgrimage of yours. But I believed, and still do, that the end of our city will come with fire and brimstone from above; and so I have made my escape."
Christian: "Did you hear no talk of our neighbor Pliable?"

Faithful: "Yes, Christian; I heard that he followed you until he came to the Slough of Despond, where, as some said, he fell in — though he would not let it be known that he had. But I am sure he was thoroughly bedraggled with that kind of dirt."
Christian: "And what did the neighbors say to him?"

Faithful: "Since his going back he has been held in great scorn, and that among all sorts of people; some mock and despise him, and scarcely anyone will give him work. He is now seven times worse off than if he had never left the city."
Christian: "But why should they be so set against him, since they also despise the way he forsook?"

Faithful: "Oh, they say, 'Hang him, he is a turncoat! He was not true to what he professed.' I think God has stirred up even his enemies to hiss at him and make him a byword, because he has forsaken the way." [Jer. 29:18,19]
Christian: "Did you have no talk with him before you came out?"
Faithful: "I met him once in the streets, but he slunk away to the other side, like one ashamed of what he had done; so I did not speak to him."

Christian: "Well, at my first setting out I had hopes of that man; but now I fear he will perish in the overthrow of the city. For it has happened to him according to the true proverb: 'The dog is turned to his own vomit again, and the sow that was washed, to her wallowing in the mire.'" [2 Pet. 2:22]
Faithful: "These are my fears for him too; but who can prevent what is to be?"

Christian: "Well, neighbor Faithful, let us leave him, and talk of things that more directly concern ourselves. Tell me now, what have you met with on the way as you came? For I know you have met with something, or else it may be set down as a wonder."
Faithful: "I escaped the Slough that I saw you fell into, and got up to the gate without that danger; only I met with one named Wanton, who nearly did me a mischief."
Christian: "It was well you escaped her net. Joseph was hard pressed by her, and escaped her as you did; but it nearly cost him his life. [Gen. 39:11-13] But what did she do to you?"
Faithful: "You can hardly imagine — unless you already know something — what a flattering tongue she had. She pressed me hard to turn aside with her, promising me all kinds of contentment."
Christian: "Well, she did not promise you the contentment of a good conscience."
Faithful: "You know what I mean — all carnal and fleshly contentment."
Christian: "Thank God you escaped her. 'The man abhorred of the Lord shall fall into her ditch.'" [Prov. 22:14]
Faithful: "Well, I am not sure whether I wholly escaped her or not."
Christian: "Why, surely you did not consent to her desires?"

Faithful: "No, I did not defile myself; for I remembered an old writing I had seen, which said, 'Her steps take hold on hell.' [Prov. 5:5] So I shut my eyes, because I would not be bewitched by her looks. [Job 31:1] Then she railed at me, and I went on my way."
Christian: "Did you meet with no other assault as you came?"

Faithful: "When I came to the foot of the hill called Difficulty, I met a very old man, who asked me what I was and where I was bound. I told him I was a pilgrim, going to the Celestial City. Then the old man said, 'You look like an honest fellow; will you be content to live with me for the wages I will give you?' Then I asked him his name, and where he lived. He said his name was Adam the First, and that he lived in the town of Deceit. [Eph. 4:22] I asked him what his work was, and what wages he would give. He told me his work was many delights, and his wages that I should be his heir at last. I asked him further what kind of house he kept, and what other servants he had. He told me that his house was furnished with all the dainties in the world, and that his servants were of his own begetting. Then I asked if he had any children. He said he had only three daughters: the Lust of the Flesh, the Lust of the Eyes, and the Pride of Life [1 John 2:16], and that I could marry them all if I wished. Then I asked how long he would have me live with him. And he told me, as long as he himself lived."
Christian: "Well, and what conclusion did you and the old man come to at last?"

Faithful: "Why, at first I found myself somewhat inclined to go with the man, for I thought he spoke very fair. But looking into his forehead as I talked with him, I saw there written, 'Put off the old man with his deeds.'"
Christian: "And then?"

Faithful: "Then it came burning hot into my mind that, whatever he said and however he flattered, once he got me home to his house he would sell me as a slave. So I told him to stop talking, for I would not come near the door of his house. Then he reviled me, and told me that he would send someone after me who would make my way bitter to my soul. So I turned to go away from him; but just as I turned, I felt him take hold of my flesh and give me such a deadly twitch backward that I thought he had pulled part of me away with him. This made me cry, 'O wretched man!' [Rom. 7:24] So I went on my way up the hill. Now when I had gotten about halfway up, I looked behind me and saw someone coming after me, swift as the wind; he overtook me just about the place where the resting-place stands."
Christian: "Just there," said Christian, "I sat down to rest, but, overcome with sleep, I lost this scroll out of my coat."

Faithful: "But, good brother, hear me out. As soon as the man overtook me, it was a word and a blow; for down he knocked me, and left me for dead. But when I came to myself a little, I asked him why he treated me so. He said it was because of my secret leaning toward Adam the First; and with that he struck me another deadly blow on the breast, and beat me down backward, so that I lay at his feet as dead as before. So when I came to myself again, I begged him for mercy; but he said, 'I do not know how to show mercy,' and with that knocked me down again. He would no doubt have made an end of me, but that one came by and told him to stop."
Christian: "Who was that who told him to stop?"
Faithful: "I did not recognize him at first, but as he went by I saw the holes in his hands and in his side; then I concluded that he was our Lord. So I went on up the hill."
Christian: "That man who overtook you was Moses. He spares no one, nor does he know how to show mercy to those who break his law."

Faithful: "I know it very well; it was not the first time he has met with me. It was he who came to me when I lived at ease at home, and told me he would burn my house over my head if I stayed there."
Christian: "But did you not see the house that stood on the top of the hill, on the side of which Moses met you?"

Faithful: "Yes, and the lions too, before I came to it; but as for the lions, I think they were asleep, for it was about noon; and because I had so much of the day before me, I passed by the porter and came down the hill."

Christian: "He did tell me he saw you go by; but I wish you had called at the house, for they would have shown you so many rare things that you would scarcely have forgotten them to your dying day. But please tell me, did you meet no one in the Valley of Humiliation?"

Faithful: "Yes, I met one Discontent, who would gladly have persuaded me to go back again with him. His reason was that the valley was altogether without honor. He told me, moreover, that to go there was to disobey all my friends — Pride, Arrogance, Self-conceit, Worldly-glory, and others — who, he said, would be very much offended if I made such a fool of myself as to wade through that valley."
Christian: "Well, and how did you answer him?"

Faithful: "I told him that although all those he named might claim kinship with me — and rightly, for indeed they were my relations according to the flesh — yet since I became a pilgrim they had disowned me, as I had also rejected them; and so they were now no more to me than if they had never been of my family. I told him, moreover, that he had quite misrepresented this valley; for 'before honor is humility,' and 'a haughty spirit goes before a fall.' Therefore, I said, I would rather go through this valley to the honor that the wisest have so accounted, than choose what he thought most worthy of our affections."
Christian: "Did you meet with nothing else in that valley?"

Faithful: "Yes, I met with Shame; but of all the men I met with on my pilgrimage, he, I think, bears the wrong name. The others would take 'no' for an answer after a little arguing, but this bold-faced Shame would never give up."
Christian: "Why, what did he say to you?"

Faithful: "What! Why, he objected against religion itself. He said it was a pitiful, low, sneaking business for a man to mind religion; that a tender conscience was an unmanly thing; and that for a man to watch over his words and ways, so as to tie himself up from the swaggering liberty that the bold spirits of the times indulge in, would make him the laughingstock of the age. He objected, too, that few of the mighty, rich, or wise were ever of my opinion [1 Cor. 1:26; 3:18; Phil. 3:7,8], nor any of them at all [John 7:48], until they were persuaded to become fools and, out of a voluntary foolishness, to risk the loss of everything for nobody-knows-what. He objected, moreover, to the base and low estate and condition of those who were chiefly the pilgrims of the times, as well as their ignorance and lack of understanding in all natural science. Indeed, he held me to it on a great many more matters than I can relate: that it was a shame to sit whining and mourning under a sermon, and a shame to come home sighing and groaning; that it was a shame to ask my neighbor's forgiveness for petty faults, or to make restitution where I had taken from anyone. He said too that religion made a man grow strange to the great, because of a few vices (which he called by finer names), and made him respect the lowly, because of the same religious fraternity. 'And is this not,' he said, 'a shame?'"
Christian: "And what did you say to him?"

Faithful: "Say! I could not tell what to say at first. Indeed, he put me to it so that the blood came up in my face; this Shame fetched it up, and had almost beaten me clean off. But at last I began to consider that 'what is highly esteemed among men is an abomination in the sight of God.' [Luke 16:15] And I thought again: this Shame tells me what men are, but it tells me nothing of what God or the Word of God is. And I thought, moreover, that at the day of doom we shall not be sentenced to death or life according to the swaggering spirits of the world, but according to the wisdom and law of the Highest. So, I thought, what God says is best, is best indeed, though all the men in the world are against it. Seeing then that God prefers his religion; seeing God prefers a tender conscience; seeing those who make themselves fools for the kingdom of heaven are the wisest; and that the poor man who loves Christ is richer than the greatest man in the world who hates him — Shame, depart! You are an enemy to my salvation. Shall I welcome you against my sovereign Lord? How then shall I look him in the face at his coming? If I should now be ashamed of his ways and servants, how can I expect his blessing? [Mark 8:38] But indeed, this Shame was a bold villain; I could scarcely shake him out of my company; he would keep haunting me, and continually whispering in my ear about one or another of the weaknesses that attend religion. But at last I told him it was useless to keep at it, for the very things he disdained were the things in which I saw the most glory. And so at last I got past this nagging fellow. And when I had shaken him off, then I began to sing:
The trials that those men do meet withal,
That are obedient to the heavenly call,
Are manifold, and suited to the flesh,
And come, and come, and come again afresh;
That now, or sometime else, we by them may
Be taken, overcome, and cast away.
Oh, let the pilgrims, let the pilgrims, then
Be vigilant, and quit themselves like men."

Christian: "I am glad, my brother, that you withstood this villain so bravely; for, as you say, I think he bears the wrong name. He is so bold as to follow us in the streets, and to try to put us to shame before all men — that is, to make us ashamed of what is good. But if he were not himself shameless, he would never attempt what he does. Let us still resist him; for, for all his bravado, he promotes nobody but the fool. 'The wise shall inherit glory,' said Solomon, 'but shame shall be the promotion of fools.'" [Prov. 3:35]
Faithful: "I think we must cry to Him for help against Shame, who would have us be valiant for the truth on the earth."
Christian: "You speak truly. But did you meet no one else in that valley?"
Faithful: "No, not I; for I had sunshine all the rest of the way through that valley, and also through the Valley of the Shadow of Death."

Christian: "It was well for you. I am sure it went far otherwise with me. For a long stretch, almost as soon as I entered that valley, I had a dreadful combat with that foul fiend Apollyon. Indeed, I truly thought he would kill me — especially when he got me down and crushed me under him, as if he would crush me to pieces; for as he threw me, my sword flew out of my hand. He even told me he was sure of me. But I cried to God, and he heard me, and delivered me out of all my troubles. Then I entered the Valley of the Shadow of Death, and had no light for almost half the way through it. I thought I would be killed there over and over; but at last day broke, and the sun rose, and I went through what was left with far more ease and quiet."

Then I saw in my dream that, as they went on, Faithful happened to look to one side and saw a man named Talkative walking at a distance beside them; for in this place there was room enough for them all to walk. He was a tall man, and somewhat better-looking at a distance than up close. To this man Faithful spoke as follows:
Faithful: "Friend, where are you headed? Are you going to the heavenly country?"
Talkative: "I am going to that very place."
Faithful: "That is good; then I hope we may have your good company."
Talkative: "With a very good will, I will be your companion."
Faithful: "Come on, then, and let us go together, and let us spend our time talking of things that are profitable."

Talkative: "To talk of things that are good is very acceptable to me, with you or with anyone else; and I am glad I have met with those inclined to such good work. For, to tell the truth, there are few who care to spend their time this way as they travel; most choose rather to talk of things that bring no profit, and this has been a trouble to me."
Faithful: "That is indeed a thing to be lamented; for what things are so worthy of the use of men's tongues and mouths on earth as the things of the God of heaven?"

Talkative: "I like you wonderfully well, for your sayings are full of conviction. And I will add: what is so pleasant, and what so profitable, as to talk of the things of God? What is so pleasant — if a man delights in things that are wonderful? For instance, if a man delights to talk of the history or the mystery of things; or if he loves to talk of miracles, wonders, or signs — where will he find anything recorded so delightful, and so sweetly penned, as in the Holy Scriptures?"
Faithful: "That is true; but to be profited by such things in our talk should be our aim."

Talkative: "That is just what I said; for to talk of such things is most profitable, for by doing so a man may gain knowledge of many things — of the vanity of earthly things, and the benefit of things above; and more particularly, a man may learn the necessity of the new birth, the insufficiency of our works, the need of Christ's righteousness, and so on. Besides, by this a man may learn, by talking, what it is to repent, to believe, to pray, to suffer, and the like; by this also a man may learn the great promises and consolations of the gospel, to his own comfort. And further, by this a man may learn to refute false opinions, to vindicate the truth, and to instruct the ignorant."
Faithful: "All this is true, and glad am I to hear these things from you."

Talkative: "Alas, the lack of this is why so few understand the need of faith, and the necessity of a work of grace in the soul, in order to eternal life; instead they ignorantly live in the works of the law, by which no man can obtain the kingdom of heaven."
Faithful: "But, by your leave, heavenly knowledge of these things is the gift of God; no man attains it by human effort, or merely by talking of it."
Talkative: "All this I know very well; for a man can receive nothing unless it is given him from heaven; all is of grace, not of works. I could give you a hundred Scriptures to confirm this."
Faithful: "Well, then," said Faithful, "what one thing shall we make the subject of our talk just now?"

Talkative: "Whatever you wish. I will talk of things heavenly or things earthly; things moral or things evangelical; things sacred or things profane; things past or things to come; things foreign or things at home; things essential or things circumstantial — provided it is all done to our profit."

Faithful: Now Faithful began to wonder; and stepping over to Christian (who had walked all this while by himself), he said to him, softly, "What a fine companion we have got! Surely this man will make a very excellent pilgrim."
Christian: At this Christian smiled modestly, and said, "This man, whom you are so taken with, will beguile twenty of those who don't know him, with that tongue of his."
Faithful: "Do you know him, then?"
Christian: "Know him! Yes, better than he knows himself."
Faithful: "Please, what is he?"
Christian: "His name is Talkative; he lives in our town. I wonder you are a stranger to him — though I suppose our town is large."
Faithful: "Whose son is he? And whereabouts does he live?"

Christian: "He is the son of one Say-well; he lived in Prating Row, and is known, by all who are acquainted with him, as Talkative of Prating Row. And in spite of his fine tongue, he is a sorry fellow."
Faithful: "Well, he seems to be a very pretty man."

Christian: "That is, to those who don't have thorough acquaintance with him; for he is best abroad — near home he is ugly enough. Your saying he is a pretty man brings to mind something I have noticed in the work of a painter, whose pictures look best at a distance, but up close are far less pleasing."
Faithful: "But I am inclined to think you're joking, because you smiled."

Christian: "God forbid that I should joke (though I smiled) about this matter, or that I should accuse anyone falsely. Let me tell you more about him. This man is for any company, and for any kind of talk; just as he talks now with you, so will he talk when he is on the ale-bench; and the more drink he has in his head, the more of these things in his mouth. Religion has no place in his heart, or house, or way of living; all he has lies in his tongue, and his religion is to make a noise with it."
Faithful: "Is that so! Then I am greatly mistaken in this man."

Christian: "Mistaken! You may be sure of it. Remember the proverb, 'They say, and do not.' [Matt. 23:3] 'For the kingdom of God is not in word, but in power.' [1 Cor. 4:20] He talks of prayer, of repentance, of faith, and of the new birth; but he knows only how to talk of them. I have been in his family, and have observed him both at home and abroad, and I know what I say of him is the truth. His house is as empty of religion as the white of an egg is of flavor. There is there neither prayer nor any sign of repentance for sin; indeed, a dumb animal, in its way, serves God better than he. He is the very stain, reproach, and shame of religion to all who know him; it can hardly have a good word in all that end of the town where he lives, because of him. [Rom. 2:24,25] The common people who know him say: 'A saint abroad, and a devil at home.' His poor family find it so; he is such a churl, and so unreasonable and abusive to his servants, that they neither know how to do anything for him nor how to speak to him. Men who have any dealings with him say it is better to deal with a stranger than with him, for they will get fairer dealing. This Talkative will, if he can, go beyond them, defraud them, beguile them, and cheat them. Besides, he brings up his sons to follow his ways; and if he finds in any of them a foolish timidity (for so he calls the first stirrings of a tender conscience), he calls them fools and blockheads, and will by no means employ them in much, or speak well of them to others. For my part, I am of the opinion that by his wicked life he has caused many to stumble and fall, and will be the ruin of many more, if God does not prevent it."

Faithful: "Well, my brother, I am bound to believe you — not only because you say you know him, but also because, like a Christian, you make your report of men fairly. For I cannot think you say these things out of ill will, but because it is just as you say."

Christian: "Had I known him no more than you, I might perhaps have thought of him as you did at first. And had I had this report only from those who are enemies to religion, I would have thought it a slander — the kind that often falls from bad men's mouths upon good men's names. But all these things, and a great many more as bad, I can prove him guilty of, from my own knowledge. Besides, good men are ashamed of him; they can neither call him brother nor friend; the very mention of his name among them makes them blush, if they know him."
Faithful: "Well, I see that saying and doing are two things, and from now on I will better observe this distinction."

Christian: "They are two things indeed, and as different as the soul and the body; for as the body without the soul is but a dead carcass, so saying, if it stands alone, is but a dead carcass too. The soul of religion is the practical part: 'Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this: to visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unspotted from the world.' [James 1:27] Talkative is not aware of this; he thinks that hearing and saying will make a good Christian, and so he deceives his own soul. Hearing is only like the sowing of the seed; talking is not enough to prove that fruit is really in the heart and life. And let us be sure of this: at the day of doom, men will be judged according to their fruit. It will not be asked then, 'Did you believe?' but, 'Were you doers, or talkers only?' — and they will be judged accordingly. The end of the world is compared to a harvest; and you know that at harvest men care for nothing but fruit. Not that anything can be accepted that is not of faith; but I say this to show you how worthless Talkative's profession will be on that day."

Faithful: "This brings to my mind that saying of Moses, where he describes the clean animal. [Lev. 11:3-7; Deut. 14:6-8] It is one that parts the hoof and chews the cud — not one that only parts the hoof, or only chews the cud. The hare chews the cud, but is unclean, because it does not part the hoof. And this truly resembles Talkative: he chews the cud, he seeks knowledge, he chews on the word; but he does not divide the hoof, he does not part from the way of sinners; rather, like the hare, he keeps the foot of a dog or a bear, and so is unclean."

Christian: "You have spoken, as far as I can tell, the true gospel sense of those texts. And I will add another thing: Paul calls some men — and great talkers, too — 'sounding brass and a tinkling cymbal'; that is, as he explains it elsewhere, things without life, giving sound. [1 Cor. 13:1-3; 14:7] Things without life — that is, without the true faith and grace of the gospel; and so, things that will never be placed in the kingdom of heaven among the children of life, even though their sound, by their talk, may be as if it were the tongue or voice of an angel."
Faithful: "Well, I was not so fond of his company at first, and I am as sick of it now. What shall we do to be rid of him?"
Christian: "Take my advice and do as I tell you, and you will find that he will soon be sick of your company too — unless God touches his heart and turns it."
Faithful: "What would you have me do?"

Christian: "Why, go to him and start some serious talk about the power of religion; and ask him plainly (after he has approved of it, as he will) whether this thing is set up in his heart, house, and way of living."
Faithful: Then Faithful stepped forward again, and said to Talkative, "Come, how are you doing now?"
Talkative: "Thank you, well. I thought we would have had a great deal of talk by this time."
Faithful: "Well, if you wish, let us begin now; and since you left it to me to set the question, let it be this: How does the saving grace of God show itself when it is in the heart of a man?"

Talkative: "I see, then, that our talk is to be about the power of things. Well, it is a very good question, and I shall be glad to answer you. Take my answer briefly, thus: First, where the grace of God is in the heart, it causes a great outcry against sin. Secondly—"
Faithful: "No, hold; let us consider one at a time. I think you should rather say: it shows itself by inclining the soul to abhor its sin."
Talkative: "Why, what difference is there between crying out against sin and abhorring it?"

Faithful: "Oh, a great deal. A man may cry out against sin out of policy, but he cannot abhor it except by a godly hatred of it. I have heard many cry out against sin in the pulpit who can yet abide it well enough in their heart, house, and conduct. Joseph's mistress cried out with a loud voice, as if she were very holy; yet she would willingly have committed uncleanness with him. Some cry out against sin even as a mother cries out against the child in her lap, calling it slut and naughty girl, and then falls to hugging and kissing it."
Talkative: "You are lying in wait to catch me, I see."
Faithful: "No, not I; I am only for setting things right. But what is the second thing by which you would prove a discovery of a work of grace in the heart?"
Talkative: "Great knowledge of gospel mysteries."

Faithful: "This sign should have been first; but first or last, it too is false. For great knowledge may be gained in the mysteries of the gospel, and yet there be no work of grace in the soul. [1 Cor. 13] Indeed, if a man has all knowledge, he may yet be nothing, and so be no child of God. When Christ said, 'Do you know all these things?' and the disciples answered, 'Yes,' he added, 'Blessed are you if you do them.' He does not lay the blessing in the knowing of them, but in the doing. For there is a knowledge that is not accompanied by doing: 'He who knows his master's will, and does it not.' A man may know like an angel and yet be no Christian; so your sign is not true. Indeed, to know is a thing that pleases talkers and boasters, but to do is what pleases God. Not that the heart can be good without knowledge, for without that the heart is worthless. There is, then, knowledge and knowledge: a knowledge that rests in the bare understanding of things, and a knowledge that is accompanied by the grace of faith and love, which sets a man on doing the very will of God from the heart. The first will serve the talker; but the true Christian is not content without the other. 'Give me understanding, and I shall keep your law; yes, I shall observe it with my whole heart.'" [Ps. 119:34]
Talkative: "You are lying in wait to catch me again; this is not for edification."
Faithful: "Well, if you please, propose another sign of how this work of grace shows itself where it is."
Talkative: "Not I, for I see we shall not agree."
Faithful: "Well, if you will not, will you give me leave to do it?"
Talkative: "You may use your liberty."

Faithful: "A work of grace in the soul shows itself either to the one who has it, or to bystanders. To the one who has it, like this: it gives him conviction of sin, especially of the defilement of his nature and the sin of unbelief (for which he is sure to be damned, if he does not find mercy at God's hand by faith in Jesus Christ). [John 16:8,9; Rom. 7:24; Mark 16:16] This sight and sense of things works in him sorrow and shame for sin. He finds, moreover, the Savior of the world revealed in him, and the absolute necessity of closing with him for life; at which he finds hungerings and thirstings after him — to which hungerings the promise is made. [Matt. 5:6; Rev. 21:6] Now, according to the strength or weakness of his faith in his Savior, so is his joy and peace, his love to holiness, and his desire to know him more and to serve him in this world. But though I say it shows itself thus to him, it is only seldom that he is able to conclude that this is a work of grace, because his corruptions now, and his abused reason, make his mind misjudge in this matter. So in the one who has this work, a very sound judgment is needed before he can, with steadiness, conclude that this is a work of grace. To others it is shown like this: first, by an experiential confession of his faith in Christ; second, by a life that matches that confession — namely, a life of holiness: heart-holiness, family-holiness (if he has a family), and conduct-holiness in the world; which in general teaches him inwardly to abhor his sin, and himself for it in secret; to suppress it in his family; and to promote holiness in the world — not by talk only, as a hypocrite or talkative person may do, but by a practical submission, in faith and love, to the power of the Word. [John 14:15; Ps. 50:23; Job 42:5,6] And now, sir, as to this brief description of the work of grace, and the discovery of it: if you have anything to object, object; if not, then give me leave to put a second question to you."
Talkative: "No, my part now is not to object, but to hear; so let me have your second question."

Faithful: "It is this: Do you experience this first part of my description? And does your life and conduct testify to it? Or does your religion stand in word and tongue, and not in deed and truth? If you incline to answer me, say no more than you know God above will say 'Amen' to — and nothing but what your conscience can justify you in. For 'not he who commends himself is approved, but whom the Lord commends.' Besides, to say I am thus and so, when my conduct and all my neighbors tell me I lie, is great wickedness."

Talkative: Then Talkative at first began to blush, but, recovering himself, replied: "You now bring in experience, conscience, and God, and appeal to him for the justification of what is said. I did not expect this kind of talk, nor am I disposed to answer such questions, because I do not count myself bound to — unless you take it upon yourself to be a catechizer; and even then, I may refuse to make you my judge. But please, will you tell me why you ask me such questions?"

Faithful: "Because I saw you forward to talk, and because I did not know that you had anything but notion. Besides, to tell you all the truth, I have heard of you, that you are a man whose religion lies in talk, and that your conduct gives this mouth-profession of yours the lie. They say you are a blot among Christians, and that religion fares the worse for your ungodly conduct; that some have already stumbled at your wicked ways, and that more are in danger of being destroyed by them. Your religion will stand alongside an ale-house, and covetousness, and uncleanness, and swearing, and lying, and the keeping of vain company. The proverb is true of you that is said of a loose woman — that she is a shame to all women; so are you a shame to all who profess the faith."
Talkative: "Since you are so ready to take up reports, and to judge so rashly as you do, I can only conclude you are some peevish or melancholy man, not fit to be talked with; and so, goodbye."

Christian: Then Christian came up and said to his brother, "I told you how it would turn out; your words and his lusts could not agree. He would rather leave your company than reform his life. But he is gone, as I said; let him go; the loss is no one's but his own. He has saved us the trouble of leaving him; for, continuing as he is (as I suppose he will), he would only have been a blot in our company. Besides, the apostle says, 'From such withdraw yourself.'"
Faithful: "But I am glad we had this little talk with him; it may be he will think of it again. However, I have dealt plainly with him, and so am clear of his blood, if he perishes."

Christian: "You did well to talk so plainly to him as you did. There is too little of this faithful dealing with men nowadays, and that is what makes religion stink in the nostrils of so many. For it is these talkative fools, whose religion is only in word, and who are loose and vain in their conduct, that — being so much admitted into the fellowship of the godly — puzzle the world, blemish Christianity, and grieve the sincere. I wish all men would deal with such as you have done; then they would either be made more conformable to religion, or the company of the saints would be too hot for them." Then Faithful said:
How Talkative at first lifts up his plumes!
How bravely doth he speak! How he presumes
To drive down all before him! But so soon
As Faithful talks of heart-work, like the moon
That's past the full, into the wane he goes.
And so will all, but he that heart-work knows.
So they went on talking of what they had seen along the way, and so made that way easy which would otherwise, no doubt, have been tedious to them; for now they were going through a wilderness.

Now when they were almost out of this wilderness, Faithful happened to look back and saw someone coming after them, and he knew him. "Oh," said Faithful to his brother, "who comes there?" Then Christian looked, and said, "It is my good friend Evangelist." "Yes, and my good friend too," said Faithful, "for it was he who set me on the way to the gate." Now Evangelist had come up to them, and greeted them like this:
Evangelist: "Peace be with you, dearly beloved; and peace be to your helpers."
Christian: "Welcome, welcome, my good Evangelist! The sight of your face brings back to my memory your old kindness and tireless labor for my eternal good."
Faithful: "And a thousand times welcome," said good Faithful. "How desirable your company is to us poor pilgrims, O sweet Evangelist!"
Evangelist: Then Evangelist said, "How has it fared with you, my friends, since the time we last parted? What have you met with, and how have you behaved yourselves?"
Then Christian and Faithful told him all the things that had happened to them on the way, and how, and with what difficulty, they had arrived at that place.

Evangelist: "I am right glad," said Evangelist — "not that you have met with trials, but that you have been victors; and that you have, in spite of many weaknesses, continued in the way to this very day. I say I am right glad of this, both for my own sake and for yours. I have sown, and you have reaped; and the day is coming when both he who sowed and they who reaped shall rejoice together — that is, if you hold out; 'for in due season you shall reap, if you faint not.' [John 4:36; Gal. 6:9] The crown is before you, and it is an incorruptible one; so run, that you may obtain it. [1 Cor. 9:24-27] Some set out for this crown, and after they have gone far for it, another comes in and takes it from them; so hold fast what you have, and let no man take your crown. [Rev. 3:11] You are not yet out of gunshot of the Devil; you have not yet resisted to the point of blood, striving against sin. Let the kingdom be always before you, and believe steadfastly concerning the things that are unseen. Let nothing on this side of the other world get within you; and above all, look well to your own hearts and the lusts thereof, 'for they are deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked.' Set your faces like a flint; you have all power in heaven and earth on your side."

Christian: Then Christian thanked him for his exhortation, but told him, too, that they would have him speak further to them, for their help the rest of the way — and the more so because they well knew he was a prophet, and could tell them of things that might happen to them, and how they might resist and overcome them. To this request Faithful also agreed. So Evangelist began as follows:

Evangelist: "My sons, you have heard, in the words of the truth of the gospel, that you must, through many tribulations, enter the kingdom of heaven; and again, that in every city bonds and afflictions await you; so you cannot expect to go long on your pilgrimage without them, in one form or another. You have already found something of the truth of these testimonies upon you, and more will follow immediately. For now, as you see, you are almost out of this wilderness, and so you will soon come to a town that you will shortly see before you; and in that town you will be hard set upon by enemies, who will strain hard to kill you; and be sure that one, or both, of you must seal with blood the testimony you hold. But be faithful unto death, and the King will give you a crown of life. He who dies there, although his death will be unnatural, and his pain perhaps great, will yet have the better of his fellow — not only because he will arrive at the Celestial City soonest, but because he will escape many miseries that the other will meet with in the rest of his journey. But when you come to the town, and find fulfilled what I have told you, then remember your friend; quit yourselves like men, and commit the keeping of your souls to your God, in well-doing, as to a faithful Creator."

Then I saw in my dream that when they had gotten out of the wilderness, they soon spotted a town ahead of them, and the name of that town is Vanity; and at the town there is a fair held, called Vanity Fair. It is kept all year long. It bears the name Vanity Fair because the town where it is held is lighter than vanity [Ps. 62:9], and also because all that is sold there, and all that comes there, is vanity — as is the saying of the wise: "all that comes is vanity." [Eccl. 1; 2:11,17; 11:8; Isa. 40:17]

This fair is no newly established business, but a thing of ancient standing; and let me tell you how it came to be. Almost five thousand years ago there were pilgrims walking to the Celestial City, as these two honest persons are; and Beelzebub, Apollyon, and Legion, with their companions, seeing by the path the pilgrims took that their way to the city lay through this town of Vanity, plotted to set up a fair here — a fair in which all sorts of vanity would be sold, and that should last all year long. So at this fair are sold such merchandise as houses, lands, trades, places, honors, promotions, titles, countries, kingdoms, lusts, pleasures, and delights of all sorts — such as harlots, wives, husbands, children, masters, servants, lives, blood, bodies, souls, silver, gold, pearls, precious stones, and what not.

And besides, at this fair there are at all times to be seen jugglings, cheats, games, plays, fools, apes, knaves, and rogues, and that of every kind. Here too are to be seen, and that for nothing, thefts, murders, adulteries, and false swearers — and that of a blood-red color.

And as in other fairs of less importance the various wares are arranged in their own rows and streets, under their proper names, so here likewise you have the proper places — rows and streets, namely countries and kingdoms — where the wares of this fair are most readily to be found. Here is the Britain Row, the French Row, the Italian Row, the Spanish Row, the German Row, where various sorts of vanities are sold. But, as in other fairs some one commodity is the chief of all, so the ware of Rome and her merchandise is greatly promoted in this fair; only our English nation, with some others, have taken a dislike to it.

Now, as I said, the way to the Celestial City lies right through this town where this lusty fair is kept; and whoever would go to the city, and yet not go through this town, "must needs go out of the world." [1 Cor. 5:10] The Prince of princes himself, when here, went through this town to his own country, and that on a fair day too; indeed, I think it was Beelzebub, the chief lord of this fair, who invited him to buy of his vanities, and would even have made him lord of the fair, if only he would have done him reverence as he went through the town. [Matt. 4:8; Luke 4:5-7] Yes, because he was such a person of honor, Beelzebub led him from street to street, and showed him all the kingdoms of the world in a little while, that he might, if possible, allure the Blessed One to cheapen and buy some of his vanities. But he had no mind for the merchandise, and so left the town without laying out so much as one penny upon these vanities. This fair, then, is an ancient thing, of long standing, and a very great fair.

Now these pilgrims, as I said, had to go through this fair. Well, so they did; but behold, even as they entered the fair, all the people in it were moved, and the town itself was in a hubbub about them, and that for several reasons.

First, the pilgrims were clothed in a kind of clothing very different from the clothing of any who traded at the fair. So the people of the fair stared at them; some said they were fools, some that they were madmen, and some that they were outlandish. [1 Cor. 4:9]

Second, just as they wondered at their clothing, so they did likewise at their speech, for few could understand what they said. They naturally spoke the language of Canaan, but those who kept the fair were the men of this world; so that, from one end of the fair to the other, they seemed barbarians to each other.

Third — and what most amused the merchants — these pilgrims set very light by all their wares; they cared not so much as to look upon them; and if the merchants called upon them to buy, they would put their fingers in their ears and cry, "Turn away my eyes from beholding vanity" [Ps. 119:37], and look upward, signifying that their trade and traffic was in heaven. [Phil. 3:20,21]

One man, noticing mockingly how the pilgrims behaved, said to them, "What will you buy?" But they, looking gravely at him, answered, "We buy the truth." [Prov. 23:23] At that there was occasion taken to despise the men the more; some mocking, some taunting, some speaking reproachfully, and some calling upon others to strike them. At last things came to a hubbub and great stir in the fair, so that all order was confounded. Now word was quickly brought to the great one of the fair, who came down and deputed some of his most trusted friends to take these men into examination, about whom the fair was almost overturned.

So the men were brought to examination; and those who sat upon them asked where they came from, where they were going, and what they were doing there in such an unusual dress. The men told them that they were pilgrims and strangers in the world, and that they were going to their own country, which was the heavenly Jerusalem [Heb. 11:13-16]; and that they had given no occasion to the men of the town, or to the merchants, thus to abuse them and stop them on their journey — except that, when one had asked them what they would buy, they had said they would buy the truth. But those appointed to examine them did not believe them to be anything but madmen, or else such as came to put all things into confusion in the fair. So they took them and beat them, and smeared them with dirt, and then put them into the cage, that they might be made a spectacle to all the men of the fair.

There, therefore, they lay for some time, and were made the objects of any man's sport, or malice, or revenge — the great one of the fair still laughing at all that befell them. But the men being patient, and "not rendering railing for railing, but rather blessing" [1 Pet. 3:9], and giving good words for bad, and kindness for the injuries done them, some men in the fair who were more observing, and less prejudiced than the rest, began to check and blame the baser sort for their continual abuse of the men. These, therefore, in an angry manner, fell upon the ones who had rebuked them, counting them as bad as the men in the cage, and telling them they seemed to be confederates and should be made to share their misfortunes. The others replied that, for all they could see, the men were quiet and sober, and intended nobody any harm; and that there were many who traded in their fair who were more worthy to be put into the cage — yes, and into the pillory too — than the men they had abused. So, after various words had passed on both sides (the men behaving themselves all the while very wisely and soberly before them), they fell to blows among themselves, and did harm to one another. Then these two poor men were brought before their examiners again, and were now charged as being guilty of the late hubbub in the fair. So they beat them pitifully, and hanged irons upon them, and led them in chains up and down the fair, as an example and a terror to others, lest any should speak on their behalf, or join themselves to them.

But Christian and Faithful behaved themselves yet more wisely, and received the disgrace and shame that was cast upon them with so much meekness and patience that it won over to their side (though they were but few in the fair) several of the men. This put the others into an even greater rage, so much so that they decided upon the death of these two men. They threatened that neither cage nor irons should serve their turn, but that they should die for the abuse they had done, and for deluding the men of the fair.

Then they were remanded to the cage again, until further order should be taken with them; so they put them in, and made their feet fast in the stocks. Here, therefore, they called again to mind what they had heard from their faithful friend Evangelist, and were the more confirmed in their way and in their sufferings by what he had told them would befall them. They also now comforted each other, that whoever's lot it was to suffer, he should have the best of it; and so each man secretly wished that he might have that preferment. But committing themselves to the all-wise disposal of him who rules all things, they remained in the condition they were in, in a contented frame of mind, until they should be otherwise disposed of.

Then, a convenient time being appointed, they brought them out to their trial, in order to their condemnation. When the time had come, they were brought before their enemies and arraigned. The judge's name was Lord Hate-good. Their indictment was one and the same in substance, though somewhat varied in form, the content being this: "That they were enemies to, and disturbers of, the trade of the town; that they had made commotions and divisions in the town, and had won a party to their own most dangerous opinions, in contempt of the law of their prince."

Then Faithful began to answer that he had only set himself against that which had set itself against him who is higher than the highest. "And," he said, "as for disturbance, I make none, being myself a man of peace. The party who were won to us were won by beholding our truth and innocence, and they have only turned from the worse to the better. And as for the king you talk of, since he is Beelzebub, the enemy of our Lord, I defy him and all his angels."

Then proclamation was made that those who had anything to say for their lord the king against the prisoner at the bar should immediately appear and give in their evidence. So there came in three witnesses: Envy, Superstition, and Pickthank. They were then asked if they knew the prisoner at the bar, and what they had to say for their lord the king against him.

Then Envy stood forth and said as follows: "My lord, I have known this man a long time, and will attest upon my oath, before this honorable bench, that he is—" "Hold! Give him his oath." So they swore him. Then he said: "My lord, this man, despite his fine name, is one of the vilest men in our country. He neither regards prince nor people, law nor custom, but does all he can to instill into all men certain disloyal notions of his own, which he generally calls principles of faith and holiness. And in particular, I myself once heard him affirm that Christianity and the customs of our town of Vanity were diametrically opposed, and could not be reconciled. By which saying, my lord, he at once condemns not only all our laudable doings, but us in the very doing of them."

Then Faithful began to reply that he had only spoken against whatever is set up against him who is higher than the highest. "And as for customs," he said, "if they are such as are contrary to the Word of God, I cannot but witness against them."

Then Superstition was sworn, and asked to say what he knew on behalf of their lord the king against the prisoner. "My lord," he said, "I have no great acquaintance with this man, nor do I desire any further knowledge of him; yet this I know, that he is a very pestilent fellow, from some talk I had with him the other day in this town; for then, as we talked, I heard him say that our religion was worth nothing, and was such by which a man could in no way please God. Which sayings of his, my lord, your lordship very well knows what must necessarily follow: that we still worship in vain, are yet in our sins, and shall finally be damned. And this is what I have to say."

Then Pickthank was sworn, and asked to say what he knew on behalf of their lord the king against the prisoner at the bar. "My lord, and you gentlemen all, this fellow I have known for a long time, and have heard him speak things that ought not to be spoken. For he has railed at our noble prince Beelzebub, and has spoken contemptibly of his honorable friends, whose names are the Lord Old Man, the Lord Carnal Delight, the Lord Luxurious, the Lord Desire of Vainglory, my old Lord Lechery, Sir Having Greedy, with all the rest of our nobility; and he has said, moreover, that if all men were of his mind, not one of these noblemen would any longer have a place to live in this town. Besides, he has not been afraid to rail on you, my lord, who are now appointed to be his judge, calling you an ungodly villain, with many other such scolding terms, with which he has bespattered most of the gentry of our town."

When this Pickthank had told his tale, the judge directed his speech to the prisoner at the bar, saying, "You runagate, heretic, and traitor, have you heard what these honest gentlemen have witnessed against you?"
Faithful: "May I speak a few words in my own defense?"
Judge: "Sirrah, sirrah! You deserve to live no longer, but to be slain on the spot; yet, that all men may see our gentleness toward you, let us hear what you, vile runagate, have to say."

Faithful: "I say, then, in answer to what Mr. Envy has spoken, that I never said anything but this: that whatever rule, or laws, or customs, or people are flatly against the Word of God are diametrically opposed to Christianity. If I have said amiss in this, convince me of my error, and I am ready here before you to retract. As to the second, Mr. Superstition, and his charge against me, I said only this: that in the worship of God there is required a divine faith; but there can be no divine faith without a divine revelation of the will of God. Therefore, whatever is thrust into the worship of God that is not in agreement with divine revelation cannot be done but by a human faith, which faith will not profit to eternal life. As to what Mr. Pickthank has said, I say (avoiding the terms of railing, of which I am accused) that the prince of this town, with all the rabble, his attendants, named by this gentleman, are more fit for a place in hell than in this town and country; and so, the Lord have mercy upon me."
